articles.title: Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services
articles.author: Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University
paras: The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service.

Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.”

Despite decades of predictions about its decline, email remains a central pillar of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world.

When most people think about cloud outages, they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service.
Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises.

When a typical cloud service breaks, it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly.
Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized “store-and-forward” architecture designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable.

Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting “send.” During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message.

From the sender’s perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn’t answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later.

One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic. Drivers miles away don’t stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system. Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate. Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site.

In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash. Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road. While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet.

When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway. The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed.

First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving. Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads.

Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet. Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days.
Long, bumpy road to recovery

Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn’t just disrupt one company; it can stall entire sectors at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response.

And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears.

articles.title: The Microsoft outage is an urgent wake-up call for greater digital resilience
articles.author: A.R.E. Taylor, Senior Lecturer in Communications, University of Exeter
paras: Friday the 13th turned out to be very unlucky indeed for Microsoft. A major outage of the tech giant’s services put a halt to digital communication for millions across the world.
So after UK government warnings to prepare for a possible cyber-attack, perhaps the bigger threat to the online world is simply the fragile design of internet infrastructure.
That fragility was plain to see on November 13. Emails and video calls stopped working as Microsoft struggled to fix “connectivity problems”.
The crash caused massive disruption to public services including hospitals and schools.

At the time of writing, what caused the outage remains unclear. But whatever it was also highlights the risks of market concentration, where a relatively small number of powerful corporations have become responsible for providing and maintaining most of the digital services on which we depend.
Microsoft has previously presented that dominance as a corporate strength. The company once claimed that serving billions of customers gives their global digital ecosystem a “unique vantage point”.
But while this level of market domination is good for business, it is not necessarily good for infrastructural resilience.

The internet has become increasingly dominated by a relatively small number of powerful corporations. The expansion of cloud computing has accelerated this centralisation, concentrating the provision of computing resources in the hands of a few major companies.
As Friday 13th demonstrated, this level of concentration can lead to widespread disruption.
And it’s not even an isolated incident.

A similar outage revealed similar risks in July 2024 when a faulty security update crashed millions of systems that used Microsoft Windows. IT systems around the world suddenly ground to a halt, leaving pharmacies, airports and banks unable to operate.

Just last month, on October 22, AI testing revealed security vulnerabilities in a programme which underpinned roughly 70% of the world’s websites. Governments and businesses took thousands of sites and online services offline to prevent potential cyber-attacks and data theft.
A month before that, autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked government infrastructure.
So there are clearly weaknesses in the current design of the internet and its enormously complex ecosystem of interdependencies.
Those ecosystems are not just chips and wires. It can be easy to forget the people who deliver the digital services we often take for granted.

The internet depends upon extensive material infrastructure and the operation of that infrastructure is not automatic. It relies on a large human workforce, which operates amid demanding schedules, tight deadlines and the pressure to maintain uninterruptible services.
As an anthropologist who conducts fieldwork in the data centre industry, I have spent a lot of time with the people who work behind the screens of the digital world.
Where organisations are understaffed or place excessive demands on their employees, the capacity to undertake comprehensive testing, monitoring and diagnostic work may be compromised.

The burden of restoring services following the Microsoft outage will fall heavily on IT professionals across the affected organisations. Many of them will be required to work demanding hours to bring the disrupted systems back online.
The physical and psychological toll that major infrastructure failures can impose on these workers remains an important dimension of the wider costs of digital disruption.
All eggs inside one digital basket

And then there’s the social cost. Sociologists of risk have long argued that the vulnerabilities of technologically advanced societies stem, in part, from their growing dependence on complex and interconnected infrastructures.
The consolidation of digital infrastructure has concentrated considerable power and responsibility in the hands of a relatively small number of private corporations.
And the Microsoft incident illustrates the extent to which organisations have come to place their operational continuity in the hands of major technology providers.
Microsoft’s infrastructure underpins an enormous range of everyday activities – activities undertaken by schools and hospitals, by businesses and charities.

When these services become unavailable, the consequences extend far beyond the immediate inconvenience of being unable to access an email account. Organisations, vital public services and even nation states which outsource essential aspects of their digital operations to a single provider can find themselves unable to function when that provider experiences a major failure.
The growing dependence on a concentrated technology ecosystem therefore raises fundamental questions about digital resilience.
As societies become increasingly reliant on online services, the consequences of infrastructure failures could become more extensive – and more damaging.

articles.title: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
articles.author: Narmin Nahidi, Assistant Professor in Finance, University of Exeter
paras: When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.

Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence?

We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences.

As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies?
The cloud has a physical footprint
The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware.

The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of global demand. It projects that consumption could reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, largely driven by AI and other digital services.

Microsoft’s own 2026 sustainability report illustrates the tension. The company reported a 25% year-over-year rise in total emissions in 2025, primarily because of expanding data centres and a change in renewable-energy certificate accounting. Microsoft is also investing in cleaner energy and more efficient infrastructure. Both facts matter: technological progress can reduce emissions per task, while growth pushes overall demand higher.
Asking the right questions

Turkey’s Cop31 presidency released the voluntary Antalya artificial intelligence pledge in October. This pledge aims to encourage climate-responsible AI while acknowledging the energy and water demands of the technology.

The World Resources Institute, a global research organisation, welcomed the pledge’s direction but warned that voluntary commitments need stronger accountability mechanisms. Meanwhile, the International Telecommunication Union has scheduled a Cop31 event for November 16 on financing cleaner digital infrastructure, measuring emissions, and promoting durable, repairable and reusable electronics.

The message is important: sustainability cannot stop at greener electricity. It also concerns what technology organisations purchase, how long they keep it, and who pays for its environmental effects.
When a software decision becomes a hardware bill

Consider a computer that still works but cannot support a newer operating system. Windows 10’s regular support ended in October 2025, although Microsoft offers extended security updates for eligible consumer devices through October 2027.
The transition does not make every older computer obsolete. Yet software support and compatibility can influence whether organisations replace otherwise usable equipment.

Manufacturing devices consumes energy and raw materials. It also creates electronic waste (e-waste). According to the UN’s global e-waste monitor, the world generated 62 million metric tonnes of e-waste in 2022, of which just 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled.
These figures cover all electronic waste, not waste attributable to Microsoft. They nevertheless show why extending equipment lifetimes deserves a place in climate policy.
Costs that are rarely counted
A software subscription has a visible price. Less visible are the costs of training employees, migrating files, replacing equipment, maintaining duplicate systems and eventually switching suppliers.
Economists call these switching costs. They can lock organisations into existing providers even when better-value alternatives emerge.

This is not merely hypothetical. In March 2026, the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority announced plans to investigate Microsoft’s business software ecosystem. It also reported steps by major cloud service providers, including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, to reduce data-transfer fees and improve interoperability, making it easier for businesses to switch between providers.

What might this have to do with sustainability? A buyer unable to change providers easily may also struggle to choose lower-emission computing services. That is a potential environmental consequence of lock-in, not a demonstrated claim that Microsoft users emit more carbon.

There is a wider accounting problem too. The UN estimates that global electronic waste was associated with approximately US$78 billion (£59 billion) in externalised costs in 2022, including pollution and climate-related impacts. Such costs are largely absent from the price of a software license.
A responsible procurement decision should therefore compare lifetime financial costs, equipment lifespans and credible emissions data rather than only the next annual bill.
Could workplaces use alternatives (such as Thunderbird and LibreOffice) or interoperable cloud services? Often, yes. But migration has costs and a rival provider is not necessarily greener.
The better goal is freedom to choose: portable data, open document formats, repairable devices, transparent environmental reporting and software contracts that do not penalise switching.
Digital systems that remain affordable, competitive and environmentally responsible, even when their preferred technology changes, will be the most resilient ones.

articles.title: ‘Race realism’: why scientifically flawed approach fails to present a realistic view of race
articles.author: Jonathan R. Goodman, Assistant Research Professor, Psychiatry, University of Cambridge
paras: At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people – which can still be found in academic journals today – are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism”. But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

What got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.

This group produces work which has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research. Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.
How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?

The Insights section is committed to high-quality longform journalism. Our editors work with academics from many different backgrounds who are tackling a wide range of societal and scientific challenges.
Scientific shortcomings: biology and genetics

Contemporary race scientists position themselves as persecuted but legitimate scientists who are prevented from pursuing their work for ideological reasons. They sometimes refer to what they defend as hereditarianism. This is the idea that genetic differences play a key causal role in determining differences in human behaviour and intelligence between human groups – such as races – over purely environmental differences.

Yet scientific evidence has shown repeatedly and from many points of view that hereditarian thinking is both flawed and wrong. Race scientists make extremely simplistic claims such as: “Black people have innately lower intelligence than white people, because selection pressures resulted in the evolution of higher intelligence in white people”. No part of this claim can be scientifically supported; not from the point of view of genetics, evolutionary biology or psychology.

In the 1970s, the influential evolutionary biologist Richard Lewontin famously showed that there is more genetic variation within human groups than between them. Socially defined racial groups just aren’t that genetically different from one another. There is genetic variation – though we’re actually a relatively genetically similar species compared to closely related primates. But this variation doesn’t fall neatly into clusters which correlate with how we typically categorise races.

Skin tone and colour do vary between geographical locations. So do some other physiological features like hair texture, or the ability to process oxygen or milk products. But these differences are associated with characteristics of the environment rather than with racial groups. Some genetic variants associated with white skin colour, for example, may have originated in Africa. Similarly, the ability to digest milk is seen in some populations in Europe, Africa and Asia, rather than being an exclusively “Aryan” characteristic, as far right groups sometimes claim.

We now know considerably more about the human genome than Lewontin did in the 1970s, but his conclusions are supported today. Knowing someone’s race just doesn’t tell us a great deal about their genetics.

Recent scientific advances allowing us to examine ancient DNA from archaeological sites help explain why genetic differences do not fall neatly along racial lines. This research paints a picture of constant mixing between human groups, as waves of migration washed to and fro across the globe. It ultimately makes any belief in the genetic “purity” of European or African populations meaningless.

While human genetics is fascinatingly complex, race scientists ignore this complexity in favour of a far-too-simplistic view of humanity. And this view is not supported by the work of scientists who have used rigorous scientific methods to further our understanding of our species.
Challenges from social science

When race scientists say that black people have lower intelligence than white people, they typically base that on claims of differences in IQ test results. But the data underlying these claims is often shaky, to say the least.

Hereditarians have relied heavily on a database which claims to provide average IQs for countries worldwide: the “national IQ” database. Researchers have repeatedly demonstrated that this database is deeply methodologically flawed. It isn’t possible to measure intelligence in the same way in very different cultures, with different exposure to formal education. That’s because we know that education is one of several other factors linked to differences in IQ.

The methods used to put the database together did not come even close to meeting typical standards of scientific rigour. There’s even analysis suggesting that low IQ samples were deliberately chosen to represent sub-Saharan Africa, to make the IQ for black populations artificially low.

Meanwhile, the Flynn effect, showing that IQ has risen considerably during the 20th and 21st centuries, clearly demonstrates that IQ scores are heavily determined by the environment we’re in. Such a rapid rise over a short period of time must have environmental, not genetic, causes.

What’s more, intelligence is a contested topic – something which is hard to define and measure. IQ tests only measure specific cognitive abilities, ignoring things like social intelligence or creativity, for example. In fact, social intelligence features heavily in mainstream research on the evolution of human intelligence.

As one of us recently outlined in a peer-reviewed paper, race scientists are largely silent on the social brain hypothesis – the view that humans evolved remarkable intellectual abilities to manage social issues. In every group, there is strong social competition around resources, mating and status. These are the things humans spend the most time navigating – the complexities of our rich social lives.

Not one of the prominent mainstream views on the evolution of human intelligence concludes there are innate cognitive differences between racial groups. Factors that have been put forward range from our cooperative child rearing to our heavy reliance on culture and learning. These all involve our social relationships and all have received equal lack of attention from race scientists.

Mainstream opinion in the evolutionary behavioural sciences is that cognitively, all human groups are the same, though of course individuals within groups differ. Our amazing behavioural diversity stems from our species’ ability to adapt flexibly to our environment. This is especially because of our reliance on culture and social learning – not because we have evolved different psychologies to suit different environments.

Rather than drawing on this mainstream research, race scientists use simplistic “just-so” stories to explain how race differences in traits such as intelligence supposedly evolved. Their “cold winters theory”, for example, claims that the challenges of cold winters in Europe and east Asia created evolutionary selection pressures for greater intelligence after human groups migrated out of Africa. In doing so, they make unsupportable assumptions about environmental differences between Africa and the rest of the world. They also fail to acknowledge half a century of research on the evolution of human cognitive ability.

Yes, we needed to learn new food gathering practices and methods for dealing with environmental challenges as we migrated across the world. But the same was true as humans migrated across the large and ecologically diverse continent of Africa. Race scientists provide no evidence for their arguments. They don’t rely on archaeological evidence, nor do they use typical methods from evolutionary biology to understand evolutionary processes. Using the methods of race scientists, it would be equally easy to make the argument that challenges posed by hot summers drove the evolution of higher intelligence, and equally without scientific backing.
No matter which way you look at these issues – from the view of genetics, anthropology, evolutionary biology or psychology – hereditarianism does not hold up.
A short history of race science

To understand the potential consequences of these views, it is important to see them in historical context. Early in the 20th century, race science was mainstream. Overly simplistic and biologically deterministic views about the origins of differences between human groups – not just race but class – were widespread (if not universal) and important to the eugenics movement.

If disadvantaged groups owe their disadvantage to some fault within them, and not to the structural conditions they experience, then some argue society is not responsible for helping those people. Such arguments led to eugenic sterilisation laws which aimed to “improve” society by preventing – without their consent – the reproduction of those considered likely to pass on their innate “defects” to future children. And it was ultimately behind the Nazis’ “solution” of trying to eliminate “undesirables” entirely.

In the decades after the second world war, the horrors of the Nazi regime led to a decline in the popularity of eugenics in mainstream research and a rejection of race science. But the belief that science supported eugenic claims was already collapsing, even as the Nazis were trying to implement a race-based society. As we learned more about human biology and genetics during the 20th century, it became obvious that human genetic variation was too complex to be mapped into socially recognised racial (or class) categories. Advances in science meant race science dropped out of mainstream thinking.

Yet those committed to a belief in a biological hierarchy of races, regardless of what the science said, wanted venues in which they could continue their discussions. In the 1960s, the pseudo-scientific journal Mankind Quarterly became their venue. Mankind Quarterly was funded by the Pioneer Fund, a non-profit foundation set up in the 1930s by a US textile magnate who chose to use his fortune to fund research on race science and fight desegregation in the US.

The Pioneer Fund continued to fund race science into the 21st century – including supporting Mankind Quarterly – when it was taken over by the current network of race scientists. They channelled its remaining funds into a new company, the Human Diversity Foundation, subsequently rebranded as Polygenic Scores LLC.
How race science still persists

Given all this, how is race science still being published in mainstream academic journals? To be clear, race science does not typically get published in genetics or evolutionary biology journals. Most academic journals operate peer review, meaning papers only get published after evaluation by experts in the field. The overall absence of race science in genetics or biology journals is a clear signal that it does not meet contemporary standards of scientific rigour in genetics or biology.

Instead, race scientists continue to publish in para-scientific journals. But race science also makes it into a growing number of mainstream social science or humanities journals. Psychologist Andrew Winston, an expert in the history of race science in psychology has described it as a “community project … with its own networks, mentorships, journals, funding, conferences, heroes, origin myths, martyrs, defenders and historiography.

Behind the network of writers producing race science sits a community of editors, peer reviewers and others in gatekeeping roles which too often allows race science to be published in mainstream journals. This is particularly in the subfields of psychology interested in intelligence and individual differences, and evolutionary psychology.

Editors of Intelligence, the mainstream journal which has probably published the largest quantity of race science, have occasionally published editorials defending their publication of race science in the name of ensuring robust academic debate even on controversial topics.

There have been sanctions. Philippe Rushton, one of an earlier generation of race scientists, faced sanctions from his university in Canada but kept his job apparently owing to the intervention of Edward O. Wilson, arguably the most famous biologist towards the end of the 20th century.

Cofnas created justified controversy over his call for a "hereditarian revolution” after which it will be acknowledged that black people are innately intellectually disadvantaged compared to white people. But he kept his postdoctoral fellowship at Cambridge University (though his affiliation with a Cambridge college was ended). He has also kept his postdoctoral position at Ghent University after using the opportunity provided by excessive news coverage of Arday to publicise his hereditarian views (though some sanctions have been imposed, such as restrictions on teaching). Cofnas has defended his views by saying he’s been misunderstood and is entitled to free inquiry.

Moreover, when University College London discovered that the race science community had been holding conferences on its premises (the “London Conferences on Intelligence”), without their knowledge of the subject of the conferences, they acted to prevent further such conferences being held. The publisher of the journal Intelligence, Elsevier, has recently appointed new editors, who have stated their commitment to publishing both rigorous and socially responsible science. Race scientists are increasingly publishing in evolutionary psychology journals rather than Intelligence.

However, the London Conferences on Intelligence continue, though not at UCL. Race scientists also have a media arm, Aporia magazine, which promotes race science using much more overt language and with more obvious policy focus than publications in academic journals. One Aporia article, for example, argued for eugenics as a solution to Africa’s lack of economic development, noting in a post that some may find it “distateful”. It claimed – relying on race science’s unscientific arguments – that artificial selection for higher intelligence is needed to improve the continent’s innately unintelligent populace.

Race science may not have the respect of the scientific community, but it does have funding and influential backers. A report by Hope not Hate revealed that the network of race scientists received significant funding from the US businessman Andrew Conru, who withdrew his funding after the report was released.
The US Ambassador to Belgium even intervened when Ghent University set up an investigation into how Cofnas was hired.

Race scientists are far from the victims they claim to be. Race scientists in this and previous generations have worked hard to ensure their messages are heard beyond academia. And in this generation, they are successfully using social media to spread their beliefs, especially Elon Musk’s X.

But what about academic freedom? Isn’t it good for science to discuss any hypothesis to ensure free exchange of ideas? Academic debate is productive only if it involves methodologically rigorous research. Science will not progress if one side of any debate consistently uses poor-quality, methodologically flawed work. Nor is it necessary to continually debate topics which have long since been settled.

We believe it is unequivocal that race science is fundamentally pseudoscience. In our view, it’s critical to call attention to not only the scientific flaws underlying this body of work but also the real target it’s aimed at: political actors and everyday readers who ultimately decide the direction that science, and society, goes in.

articles.title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
articles.author: Linggong Kong, Ph.D. Candidate in Political Science, Auburn University
paras: Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”

Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies. She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.
Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair. And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him, he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.

The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked.
Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose.
Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “beauty stratagem.”

As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations, I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors.
The beauty stratagem of Ancient China

“Meiren ji” is one of “Thirty-Six Stratagems,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership.
The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience.
Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history.

In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge.
According to the ancient historical text “Wu Yue Chun Qiu,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs.
The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu.
Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery.
Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly.
A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “Romance of the Three Kingdoms,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature.

It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo.

The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor.
The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware

In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “honey trap.” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War.

Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu. The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s.

A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office.
Why Jensen Huang is strategically important

Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power.
Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development. Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers.
From Beijing’s perspective, advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition.
This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang.

However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation.
Espionage in the age of AI

Yet it is surely true that in modern politics – just as in ancient China’s rivalries – rivals seek information about opponents, try to influence important decisions and exploit weaknesses to gain strategic advantages.
What has changed is who controls important strategic resources.

In ancient China, influencing a ruler through personal relationships could affect a country’s political and military decisions. Today, approaching a major technology executive could offer access to sensitive technologies.
More than 2,000 years ago, a powerful state could lose its advantage through a ruler’s personal weaknesses. Today, political and technological power are distributed differently.
But as long as important decisions depend on individuals, personal relationships may remain a weakness that rivals can exploit.

articles.title: New physics machine at Cern could unlock the secrets of the electron
articles.author: Benjamin Smith, PhD Candidate in Theoretical Particle Physics, University of Glasgow
paras: The behaviour of every atom, and so all of biology and chemistry as we know them, depends on the mass of the electron.

Electrons are one of the fundamental particles (the very smallest building blocks of nature) that make up the atom. They orbit the atom’s central nucleus, which is made up of proton and neutron particles. The mass of the electron is very small, contributing little to the mass of the atom, but it is vital for determining an atom’s size.

If the mass of the electron was made significantly lighter or heavier, it would affect not only the size of the atom, but also the way that chemistry works throughout the universe – potentially making biology impossible.
Physicists have never confirmed how the electron acquires its mass. But a proposed collider at Cern, in Geneva, could finally put that to the test.

The masses of fundamental particles span an enormous range. The current best theory to explain fundamental physics, known as the Standard Model, offers no explanation for this. So testing the origin of particle masses offers a crucial check on this theory. It could also point researchers towards new discoveries in physics.

In 1964, the Edinburgh-based physicist Peter Higgs and fellow researchers proposed that fundamental particles obtain their mass by interacting with a new field. In physics, a field is a physical quantity that has a value assigned to each point in space and time, like the temperatures dotted across a weather map. An object interacting with a field is influenced by the field’s value at its location.

The stronger the interaction between a fundamental particle and this field, the heavier the particle will be. This idea became the heart of the Standard Model. It took nearly 50 years, and the construction of the largest machine ever built – the Large Hadron Collider at Cern, the European laboratory for particle physics – to confirm the existence of the Higgs boson.

The discovery of this particle confirmed that nature uses the mass-generating mechanism proposed by Peter Higgs and others back in the 60s. This momentous achievement led to Higgs and fellow pioneering physicist François Englert sharing the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Fundamental particles, like the electron, cannot be broken down into smaller parts. But they can combine to form composite particles, such as the proton and neutron that form the nucleus of an atom. The Standard Model describes twelve fundamental matter particles.
Six are called quarks and include the “up” and “down” quarks that make up protons and neutrons. The other six are called leptons, one of which is the electron.

The masses of these fundamental particles have a puzzling hierarchy. For example, the heaviest, the top quark, has a mass 300,000 times larger than the electron, and 40 times larger than the next heaviest quark.

While the Standard Model can explain how particles obtain mass, it offers no explanation for why these masses span such an enormous range. This is one of several reasons why particle physicists believe that there must be physics beyond the Standard Model that has not yet been explored.

New theories could modify our picture of how fundamental particles obtain mass, making it important to use experiments to test the mechanism proposed by Higgs and others. At the Large Hadron Collider, we have verified it for the heaviest particles, and we are close to doing so for the muon, a heavier cousin of the electron.

However, the electron interacts incredibly weakly with the Higgs field, making it too difficult to measure at current colliders. This leaves open the question of whether the Higgs mechanism is responsible for its mass.

To close this gap in our knowledge, physicists have proposed using FCC-ee, the first stage of a planned $19 billion physics machine called the Future Circular Collider, which could follow the Large Hadron Collider in the 2040s.

Most fundamental particles have a corresponding antiparticle – another sub-atomic particle that has the same mass but a different electric charge. FCC-ee would accelerate electrons and their corresponding antiparticles (known as positrons) around a 91km-long ring underneath the French-Swiss border, before colliding the two beams of particles inside detectors. These detectors are specialised experiments that can track and measure the particles produced when the beams crash into one another.

FCC-ee has a key advantage over proton-proton colliders such as the Large Hadron Collider: smashing together electrons and positrons can directly produce a Higgs boson. By looking for this process, we can probe the strength of the electron-Higgs interaction.

In principle, the measurement is simple: collide electrons with positrons and count the Higgs bosons produced. In practice, it is very challenging. To produce enough Higgs bosons, the collider would need to run for a few years at an energy extremely close to the mass of the Higgs boson particle.

However, that’s a long time to run this machine in such a specialised way. The measurement also relies on us knowing the Higgs mass much more precisely than we do today. Detecting the Higgs bosons is another challenge, because many unrelated processes can mimic the desired signal.

In a recent preprint (which has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal) on this topic, a team of physicists assumed that the Higgs bosons decay (or transform) into W bosons, another fundamental particle with a lower mass. They used a machine learning algorithm to distinguish the desired signal from other processes. In simulations, they found that this approach could improve sensitivity to the electron-Higgs interaction by nearly a factor of 200 compared with current limits at the Large Hadron Collider.

However, new theories could modify interactions between the electron and the Higgs field, including through the action of previously undiscovered particles. But these theories would also need to fit with the known, previously measured properties of the electron. This is what my collaborators and I studied in a recent paper, where we examined how new particles can change the way the electron interacts with the Higgs field.

Our findings suggest that many candidates for such hypothetical particles, such as new, heavy versions of the electron, can be indirectly searched for in planned measurements of the magnetic properties of the electron. These tests will be carried out by several different physics experiments around the world.

However, one potential new particle is a different form of the Higgs boson that interacts mainly with electrons. If this exists, the Future Circular Collider will be in a unique position to test its properties and how it affects the electron.

This story captures the interplay between theory and experiment when planning new colliders. Theorists map out the new physics a measurement could detect, so experimentalists know when a result would be decisive.

This proposed run of the FCC-ee isn’t yet confirmed and many of the new physics models it could test can be probed in other ways. But a new, electron-loving form of Higgs boson would first show up here. Either way, this measurement would tell us something we’ve never known: how the electron, one of the most studied particles in nature, truly gets its mass.
Benjamin Smith is supported by a Lord Kelvin Adam Smith scholarship from the University of Glasgow.

articles.title: How UK scientists are helping the MMX space mission grab the best sample of soil from Mars’ moon Phobos
articles.author: Chrysa Avdellidou, Lecturer in Planetary Science, School of Physics and Astronomy, University of Leicester
paras: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, but their origins remain uncertain. Were they asteroids captured by Mars’ gravity, or did they form from debris following a giant impact on the planet?

Japan’s Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission aims to solve this mystery by collecting samples of soil from Phobos, the largest of the two moons. Laboratory experiments in the UK are helping prepare scientists to interpret its findings.

MMX launched successfully on October 19 atop an H3 rocket from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan. About two weeks ago, ground controllers received the first signal from the spacecraft to check it is communicating normally.
Studying small bodies and comparing them with meteorites – natural samples of space rocks that reach Earth – helps scientists understand the formation and evolution of the Solar System.

Observations from the Soviet Union’s Phobos 2 spacecraft, which gathered data from its position in Martian orbit in 1989, and by researchers using Nasa’s Infrared Telescope Facility in the 2010s, have provided important hints about Phobos’ origins.

They showed that the Martian moon has spectral properties (the way a planetary surface absorbs and reflects light, providing information about its composition) resembling those of dark, primitive asteroids known as D-types. These are thought to have originated in the outer Solar System before some migrated towards the Sun.

For Mars to have captured two separate asteroids would be difficult to explain. An alternative proposal suggests that Mars captured fragments of an asteroid torn apart by its gravity. These fragments subsequently formed a disc of material from which the moons evolved.

However, this raises the question of how an object from the distant outer Solar System reached Mars. Another theory proposes that Phobos and Deimos formed from debris ejected into orbit when a large object struck Mars.

Although this scenario can explain aspects of their orbits, questions remain about whether their composition matches that expected from such an impact. Distinguishing between these possibilities is a major goal of the MMX mission, which will investigate both moons and return samples from Phobos to Earth.
What if Phobos contains material from elsewhere? Mars’ largest moon may hold another important clue: material delivered from another part of the Solar System.

Large impacts on Mars can eject rocks into space, some of which could eventually land on Phobos. Asteroids striking the moon directly could also leave fragments behind. Scientists call this exogenous material.

About ten years ago, I investigated this process through laboratory experiments and numerical simulations. My research demonstrated that objects colliding with another planetary body can leave material on a target’s surface even at relatively low-impact velocities.

Years later, Nasa’s Osiris-Rex mission to the asteroid Bennu and Japan’s Hayabusa2 mission to the asteroid Ryugu identified foreign material associated with impacts on their target asteroids. Finding fragments of rock from Mars or asteroid fragments on Phobos could similarly help reconstruct the moon’s impact history and shed light on its origin.

In 2023, I was selected as a participating scientist in the MMX mission and joined its surface science and geology SST (science strategy team). My research focuses on the processes shaping the moons’ surfaces, particularly impacts.

By combining observations from different spacecraft instruments, I aim to study crater numbers and sizes to understand the moons’ impact histories. I also want to establish whether foreign material can be identified on Phobos.

If the captured-asteroid theory is correct, MMX will be investigating a primitive object that formed in the outer Solar System. If the moons formed following a giant impact on Mars, they could still contain fragments of rock from Mars and the object that collided with it. This may be evident in the distinct compositions of material collected by MMX from Phobos.

Laboratory experiments have already been helping scientists predict what the MMX spacecraft’s instruments might detect. With financial support from Europlanet, a society that supports planetary scientists, I launched an experimental campaign at the University of Kent.

The tests used a light-gas gun (an apparatus that propels objects at high velocities) to fire projectiles at material designed to simulate the surface of Phobos under both proposed formation scenarios.
We investigated how crater formation depends on impact velocity and the size of the object. We also tested whether material ejected from Mars could contaminate Phobos.

Our experiments demonstrated that this process is feasible under the conditions that applied during the experiment. These tests can replicate the natural process and impact speeds. This work is being submitted to the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS).

Together with early-career scientists Dr Emelia Branagan-Harris of the University of Oxford, Dr Ben Rider-Stokes from The Open University and Dr Vassi Spathis of the Institute for Space in Leicester, we also investigated whether MMX’s instruments could detect grains of material from Mars within Phobos’ surface layer before the spacecraft collects samples. This work is currently under revision in MNRAS.

If foreign material can be identified remotely, scientists will be better equipped to interpret observations and select soil samples that will provide the most useful information. We presented our findings at the Europlanet Science Congress in The Hague, Netherlands, in September.
What comes next? At the University of Leicester, our team of scientists – called Hard Rocks – is designing experiments to investigate the potential presence of organic matter on Phobos.

Organic compounds are not necessarily evidence of life, they can also form through non-biological processes or be delivered by asteroids. But they can tell us much about the history of Phobos, adding to our understanding of how the Martian moons formed and evolved.

Whether they are captured asteroids or remnants of a giant impact, their surfaces and returned samples could reveal important clues about their formation. If Phobos also preserves material delivered from Mars or distant asteroids, these tiny moons could tell a much bigger story about the collisions and movements of material that shaped our Solar System.

articles.title: You likely have genes that affect how well your medications work – testing for them could improve treatment
articles.author: Philip Empey, Associate Professor, University of Pittsburgh School of Pharmacy, University of Pittsburgh
paras: All people carry differences in their DNA that could affect how they respond to medication, according to my team’s newly published research. Moreover, 1 in 4 already take a medication their body processes differently because of their genetics.

Clinicians often take a trial and error approach to prescriptions. Two people take the same medicine at the same dose. One starts feeling better, but the other experiences side effects or sees little benefit. For some medications, part of the reason behind that difference in response is written in a person’s DNA.

The field of pharmacogenomics studies how variations in your DNA contribute to how your body processes and responds to medicines. For instance, genes can influence how quickly your liver breaks down a drug and how long it stays in your bloodstream.

But using genetic testing to guide prescriptions is not yet routine. Part of the problem is a lack of large population data to study this approach more broadly. Clinicians don’t know when it’s best to order genetic testing. And because most genetic research has been done on people of European ancestry, researchers know less about how common key gene variants are in everyone else.
Genetic variants and drugs

To improve the diversity of pharmacogenomic data, my team of researchers and I analyzed the whole genome sequences and health records of nearly 100,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program. All of Us is an effort from the National Institutes of Health to study the health of 1 million or more people across the U.S. and its territories, with a focus on groups historically left out of biomedical research.

We examined 16 genes with well-established links to how someone responds to different medications, pairing this data with electronic health records to identify which drugs participants had already taken.

We found that every participant carried at least one relevant genetic variant, and many carried several. Around 99.5% of participants had a genetic variant for which the Food and Drug Administration or medical guidelines recommend a different drug or change in dose for certain medications.

Even more telling, about 24% had taken a drug that is affected by a genetic variant they carried. Common examples included drugs used to reduce excess stomach acid, such as omeprazole and pantoprazole, and statins used to lower cholesterol levels. Because health records can be incomplete, our results likely underestimate the actual prevalence of these gene-drug interactions.

These findings can help improve the databases clinicians and researchers use routinely in research. We identified 17,704 previously unreported variants in the regions of these genes that encode proteins. Computer models predicted that about a quarter may have significant effects on how the body processes drugs.
Our team also reported the frequencies of hundreds of genetic variants linked to drug response for people from genetic ancestries that previously had incomplete data.
Improving precision medicine

Overall, our research shows that DNA variation is very common, and broader genetic testing may help optimize the medications clinicians prescribe to patients. It’s also an example of how big initiatives such as the All of Us Research Program can advance precision medicine.

However, this study doesn’t prove testing would improve outcomes for each of these people. Additionally, genes are only one factor; age, kidney and liver function, and other medications also affect how the body processes drugs.
Still, I believe the direction of the research is clear. Pharmacogenomics can provide potentially relevant benefits for many people who take medications.

articles.title: Democrats are at Cop31 to show that the US has not abandoned the fight against climate change
articles.author: Natasha Lindstaedt, Professor in the Department of Government, University of Essex
paras: The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party.

Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?

The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 Cop conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering.
Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Being on the ground at Cop is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.

Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the Cop31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip.

During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles.

Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act.

On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend Cop summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.
Data centres are big issue

The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all.

Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions.

After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”.
Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy.

However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at Cop nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be.

The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023.

Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives.

They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this.
What does this mean globally?

What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at Cop with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies.

Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution.

While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power.

articles.title: Why the doomsday prediction of 1960 matters today
articles.author: Mark Woolhouse, Professor of Infectious Disease Epidemiology, University of Edinburgh
paras: According to the late Heinz von Foerster, Friday, November 13 2026, is doomsday. Professor von Foerster and two colleagues at the University of Illinois published that prediction in 1960 in the respected journal Science. The paper has been widely discussed ever since.

Theirs was an unconventional vision of doomsday, brought about by the world’s population growing ever faster. Eventually, there would be an infinite number of people – literally, according to the paper. As von Foerster put it, his descendants would be “squeezed to death”.

Von Foerster deliberately engineered his analysis to make this outcome inevitable. He devised a mathematical equation that was predetermined to give the desired result and fitted it to human population data over the past two millennia to come up with a precise date. November 13 2026, would have been his 115th birthday.

The paper was von Foerster’s way of making the point that the rate of human population growth in 1960 was unsustainable. That conclusion was not new – it dates back to Thomas Malthus’s 18th-century Essay on the Principle of Population. The problem was von Foerster’s proposed solution: birth control on a massive scale.

Others reached similar conclusions. In 1968, Paul Ehrlich, an American biologist and environmentalist, wrote his bestselling book The Population Bomb. He predicted mass famine. Four years later came The Limits to Growth, a report based on a computer model predicting systemic collapse by the 2020s as the growing population exhausted the planet’s resources.

These predictions turned out to be wildly wrong, but not before egregious harm was done in the name of saving the planet. During the 1970s, international agencies aggressively promoted birth control, even making it a condition of receiving food aid. Forced sterilisation programmes were introduced in south Asia. China’s one-child policy persisted until 2015.
All of these programmes were abandoned, yet the number of people aged under 15 in the world still peaked in 2021. Many countries are now concerned about their ageing populations.

Japan, Hungary, Turkey and even China are encouraging couples to have more children. This is as far as it could be from the future that von Foerster and like-minded population pessimists were imagining in the 1960s.

Some regard the doomsday paper as a historical curiosity to be regarded with indulgence. I disagree. I see it as a cautionary tale that undermines confidence in scientific predictions of all kinds. It should be cause to reflect on the merits of today’s prophecies of disaster.
Last month, a high-profile report identified 17 “major catastrophic threats”, two with “extinction potential” (nuclear war and malicious use of AI), and forecast their impacts to the year 2100.

If this type of exercise is really more credible than the population growth predictions, then the difference needs to be made plain. A good place to start is to take on board five lessons from von Foerster’s paper.

First, there is an uneasy relationship between science and advocacy. Science is about informing the debate; advocacy is about winning it. A favoured tool of the advocate is the worst-case scenario, and doomsday is the ultimate worst-case scenario. It is a rhetorical device rather than a serious scientific argument.

Second, exaggerating for effect is poor science and ultimately counterproductive. As studies of public attitudes to science have shown, people lose trust in scientists when they suspect them of overreaching.

Third, the doomsday equation illustrates a general principle: the way a model is constructed predetermines the possible outcomes. Von Foerster used this to his advantage and manufactured an eye-catching result. The same is true of many other predictions, though not usually so blatantly. No model of a complex system is exempt.

Fourth, claims to be “following the science” can discourage legitimate debate and direct attention away from the subjective choices scientists make when constructing their models. Those dire predictions of accelerating population growth were seen as incontrovertible at the time, and sceptics were accused of wilfully denying the disaster that would inevitably follow. That was pure hubris.

Fifth, ignoring inconvenient evidence will backfire, eventually. Von Foerster and the others failed to take into account that people living in richer, healthier and better-educated societies would have fewer children, to the extent that the decreasing birth rate outweighed the decreasing death rate.
This “demographic transition” was already under way by 1960 and it fatally undermined the population pessimists’ argument. Development was the answer to the population explosion.

The latest doomsday will pass uneventfully, but there’s always another waiting round the corner – it’s a recurring theme of human history. Scientists may have taken the mantle from prophets and mystics, but are they really any better?

The “scientific” predictions of population growth of the 1960s and 70s proved no more reliable than the doom-mongering of Nostradamus. There are too many parallels between that episode and today’s predictions for any complacency.

Many of today’s scientists are genuinely and deeply worried about global threats (my own top concern is another pandemic). There is a wealth of scientific evidence and opinion underpinning those fears. Even so, it would be irresponsible to ignore the lessons of recent history and risk making the same mistakes again.

Friday, November 13 2026, is an opportunity for scientists to reflect that, when it comes to prediction, a little humility goes a long way. Anyone who interrogates predictions of catastrophe is doing due diligence, and good scientists should welcome it.

articles.title: The supermarket fridge hack exposes the cracks in tech vision of an ‘internet of things’
articles.author: Vincent Charles, Professor of AI for Business and Management Science, Queen's University Belfast
paras: Imagine opening a supermarket in the morning to find the freezer aisle dripping, the floor wet, and thousands of euros’ worth of food ruined.

That is what happened in France overnight on 11-12 October 2026, when hackers remotely manipulated refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets. Temperatures reportedly reached 50°C, spoiling food worth millions of euros.

The attacks spread. In early November, similar incidents affected supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden. Food suppliers in the UK were also targeted. A London wholesaler narrowly avoided losing its stock by disconnecting affected equipment from the internet.

On Monday November 9, French officials accused Iran of being behind the attacks in France. Others, including cybersecurity experts, have previously suspected Russian involvement – something Moscow has denied.

Whoever is responsible, these incidents reveal an uncomfortable reality: cyberattacks are no longer confined to stolen passwords, compromised bank accounts or leaked information. They can disrupt the physical systems on which everyday life depends.
A term, the “internet of things”, is sometimes used for the increasing trend for physical objects to be embedded with sensors and communicating with other devices or systems over the internet.

But as more devices become connected to the internet, the question is not simply how hackers managed to heat supermarket freezers, but who is responsible for keeping these devices – and others like them – secure.
Modern supermarket refrigeration systems often use control panels that allow engineers to monitor temperatures, receive alerts, and adjust settings remotely.

The control panels operate electronic devices called controllers that manage the refrigeration systems and can be accessed remotely via the internet. This is useful: a failing freezer in the middle of the night can cause substantial losses and remote monitoring can help prevent it.
But the same connectivity that makes these systems convenient can also create opportunities for attackers.

Attackers reportedly extended defrost cycles from around one hour to eight hours, delaying alarms while temperatures rose. The concern is that equipment can remain mechanically functional long after its cybersecurity protections become inadequate.
And the implications extend beyond supermarkets. Hospitals, pharmacies, and warehouses depend on refrigeration, while connected systems also manage heating, ventilation and other building functions.

Perhaps the most revealing aspect of these attacks is their potential scale. Hackers need not target supermarkets individually. They can search the internet for particular controllers for appliances, such as fridges and freezers, and attempt to exploit the same weaknesses across businesses and countries.

Since the attacks, there has been evidence that refrigeration controllers have been disappearing from the internet, consistent either with the companies taking action to protect them, or owners disconnecting the appliances. Yet more than 3,100 remained visible online on November 5 2026. Exposure does not necessarily mean vulnerability, but it illustrates the scale of the shared risk.

A refrigeration controller may accept a change to its defrost settings even when the resulting temperatures could destroy food. Businesses therefore need more than protection against unauthorised access. Critical operating limits should be protected against dangerous remote changes, with independent safeguards and local controls – allowing supermarket employees to adjust refrigeration equipment – if digital systems are compromised.

Secure connectivity is another part of the solution. In January 2026, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre published guidance on how industrial systems connect to external networks and how those connections should be controlled.

But securing these systems also raises a question of responsibility. A supermarket may buy equipment from one company, use another for maintenance and depend on a third for software support. When vulnerabilities emerge, responsibility can become fragmented. This can leave critical security gaps unaddressed.

International cybersecurity agencies are urging organisations to consider security when purchasing industrial equipment, including manufacturers’ commitments to security updates and support throughout a product’s lifespan. This approach is known as “secure by demand”.

But what happens when an attack succeeds despite these precautions? A supermarket may suffer the immediate losses, even when the weakness lies in equipment or software supplied by someone else. Insurance may cover some of the damage, but who ultimately bears the cost depends on contracts, liability and the terms of the insurance policy. Financial risk may be transferred between organisations, but responsibility for preventing and managing cyberattacks is not necessarily transferred with it.
What about the rest of us?
The same risks increasingly extend into our homes. Smart thermostats, security cameras, doorbells and connected appliances create ongoing dependencies on their manufacturers.

Unlike traditional appliances, connected devices may rely on software updates and cloud services long after purchase. A device can become insecure before it becomes unusable. And if its manufacturer withdraws support or shuts down a cloud service, some functions may stop working altogether.
Before buying connected technology, we should ask: how long will security updates be provided? Will essential functions work without internet access? What happens when support ends?
But consumers cannot reasonably assess every vulnerability or control manufacturers’ decisions. Responsibility for security cannot rest with them alone.
We routinely ask what connected technology can do for us. Perhaps we should also ask who bears the risks when things go wrong, and who remains responsible for keeping it secure as it gets older.
