articles.title: What are biomarkers? A biologist explains how doctors measure your health – and how combining cells from different people can find new markers
articles.author: Michael F. Wells, Assistant Professor of Human Genetics, University of California, Los Angeles
paras: A family of five is exposed to the flu virus, but only two of them get sick. A lifelong chain-smoker lives 100 years, while a professional athlete in their prime dies of an unexpected heart attack. A drug fails a clinical trial due to harmful side effects in a subset of patients despite showing good results in others.
Could any of these scenarios have been predicted? The simple answer is not yet – but perhaps soon with the help of biomarkers.

A biomarker is anything measurable in the body that gives clinicians insight into someone’s current or future health. Biomarkers come in many forms and play a critical role in modern medicine by shedding light on the inner workings of the human body.
Many biomarkers are measured during routine procedures at the doctor’s office, including through blood tests and vital signs.

Physiological biomarkers such as heart rate and blood oxygen levels indicate how well your body is functioning. Cellular biomarkers such as white blood cell count provide useful information on the activity of your immune system. Genetic biomarkers are parts of your DNA that provide clues about your inherent risk of developing a particular disease or how likely you are to respond to a treatment.
There are still many more biomarkers to be discovered, and researchers are devising unique ways to identify a person’s risk of disease.
Discovering new biomarkers

The traditional way researchers identify biomarkers is by asking which biological features differ between two or more groups. This might look like comparing patients with a specific disease with healthy volunteers, people who respond to a drug with people who don’t, or the same group of people at two different points in time.

Many biomarker discoveries started with observations made in laboratories. For example, doctors use hemoglobin A1c levels in the blood to test for diabetes. The origins of this test date back to the 1960s, when scientists found abnormally high levels of a protein in the blood of diabetics. Repeated testing in the clinic over the next few decades confirmed the relationship between A1c levels and diabetes, culminating in the Food and Drug Administration approving the first A1c-based diabetes diagnostic test in 2013.

Other biomarkers that also started with observations made through basic research in the lab include screening tests for colorectal cancer, drug metabolism and inherited metabolic diseases in newborns.

Genetic biomarkers are typically found by scanning the genomes of thousands to even millions of people for genetic variants linked to a trait or disease. This approach is called a genomewide association study. This method has resulted in many important biomarkers that provide guidance on how to manage a patient’s risk of heart disease, age-related vision loss and liver disease.

One limitation of using the genomewide association study, though, is that it does not always provide information on which tissue or cell types may be relevant to the genetic variant. This lack of cellular information could be solved with cell cultures that allow researchers to study specific cell types under controlled conditions outside the body.
Human populations in a dish

In my work as a neuroscientist and geneticist, I take a different approach to finding biomarkers in the lab: I conduct genomewide association studies on human brain cells in a dish to understand how cells change when they encounter harmful exposures such as toxins and viruses.
Cells are the building blocks of all human tissues and organ systems. How sensitive they are to different environmental factors can greatly affect a person’s health and disease risk.

Thanks to revolutions in stem cell technologies, scientists are now able to model the effects of the environment on many different cell types – including brain cells that are nearly impossible to study in living people without causing irreversible damage to the brain. Instead, my colleagues and I obtain stem cells created from the blood or skin of human donors and convert them to brain cells for our experiments.

Most studies focus on how cells from only a handful of people respond to environmental stressors, mainly because it is quite difficult to conduct experiments at the population scale in a petri dish. To know whose cells are in a dish, researchers traditionally needed to handle and maintain cells from different people separately. This requirement adds considerable time, effort and cost for every new cell line included in the experimental design.

Because these issues limit the scale of experiments, studies aren’t able to capture the natural diversity of people and therefore cannot answer questions about why an exposure might make one person sick but have no effect on another.

My laboratory tackles this problem by pooling stem cell-derived brain cells from dozens to hundreds of people into the same culture dish – what my team calls a cell village. We use the genomes of these cells as natural barcodes to determine who donated each one. We then add different environmental perturbations to the village – such as pathogens, chemical pollutants and radiation – and measure how each person’s cells reacts.

Each cell might respond by turning on or off a set of genes, showing an increased or decreased propensity to die, or do nothing at all. Identifying which genes are linked to these particular responses can help explain why a person’s cells respond the way they do.
These genes are essentially biomarkers for the vulnerability of a specific cell type to an exposure.
An atlas of human vulnerability
While cell villages are relatively new, they have already helped researchers better understand what makes people different from each other.

For example, my team and I used cell villages to identify a biomarker that indicates a person may be particularly vulnerable to Zika virus infection. Zika is a pathogen spread by mosquitoes that can cause neurological disorders and microcephaly – small head size – in developing fetuses. Using stem cell-derived brain cells from 40 people, we found that not everyone was equally susceptible to infection. For some, fewer than 1% of their cells were infected by Zika virus; for others, it was greater than 99%.

Through additional cell village experiments, we discovered a genetic variant that regulates a powerful antiviral gene called IFITM3. In this case, the cells of a person with version A of this gene were more vulnerable to infection than the cells of a person with version B. Researchers have found links between this same genetic variant and COVID-19 and influenza A infection severity, suggesting it could be a genetic biomarker that can predict how certain people may respond to certain types of pathogens.

My team has also conducted similar work to identify genetic biomarkers for a person’s sensitivity to lead, a pervasive neurodevelopmental toxin. We are also using cell villages to find biomarkers for a person’s vulnerability to PFAS, also known as forever chemicals; measles virus infection; and stress hormones.
Our goal is to build what we call an atlas of human vulnerability: a catalog of genetic biomarkers to predict how each person might respond at the cellular level to a wide range of harmful exposures.
The cell village is only one of many emerging technologies that could usher in a new era of biomarker detection.

As DNA sequencing costs continue to drop, whole genome sequencing could become more routine in the clinic and potentially improve the ability to find links between genes and health outcomes that healthcare teams can intervene in.

Researchers are developing AI tools to survey medical imaging such as CT and MRI scans with the intention of finding new biomarkers for cancer progression that would have likely gone unnoticed by the human eye.

Cellphones and smartwatches may also be useful in efforts to discover new health-related biomarkers. For example, some studies have used these and other wearable devices to find behavioral biomarkers that predict major depressive episodes.

The goal now is to test how well these biomarkers work in the real world and make them widely available so that doctors everywhere can have as much information as possible about their patients when making life-changing decisions.

articles.title: Why Donald Trump keeps threatening Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain – and why it is so hard to destroy
articles.author: Arash Beidollahkhani, Research Fellow at the Global Development Institute, University of Manchester
paras: Iran has become a test of Donald Trump’s credibility at home as well as his power abroad.

The war and rising fuel prices contributed to the Republican defeat in the recent congressional elections. That gives the president a stronger political reason to find an ending to the conflict that he can present as a success.
On November 9, President Trump said he wanted to keep the war at “status quo”, but warned that American forces were “locked and loaded” should circumstances change.

One mountain near Iran’s main nuclear complex sits at the centre of America’s conundrum. Trump has repeatedly threatened Pickaxe Mountain, saying in October that the US could destroy it quickly. The gap between that promise and what a strike could achieve deserves attention.

Pickaxe Mountain is the English nickname for Kūh-e Kolang Gaz Lā, a 1,600m tall (5,200ft) peak located around 1 mile south of the Natanz nuclear complex in central Iran. Experts believe it hosts a nuclear facility, but it is thought to be much deeper than Natanz. According to experts, the complex is located between 80m and 100m underground. This makes it more difficult to destroy than other sites associated with Tehran’s nuclear programme.

The decision to build a complex at Pickaxe Mountain followed a series of explosions across Iran in 2020. These damaged alleged missile sites, power plants and other facilities. The causes remain unclear.

One blast, on July 2, 2020, damaged a workshop at the Natanz nuclear complex that was used for assembling centrifuges. These centrifuges are containers used to produce enriched uranium. The uranium can be used for civilian nuclear power plants, but is also a component in nuclear weapons. In September of that year, the head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organization said the workshop’s replacement would be built “in the heart” of Pickaxe Mountain.

The Trump administration’s concern is that Pickaxe Mountain could shelter centrifuges capable of enriching uranium to weapons grade levels. Analysts also suggest that the underground complex could accommodate other work related to developing a nuclear weapon.

Newspaper reports citing Israeli intelligence assessments claim that Iran moved centrifuges and related equipment into its tunnels. The mountain could also provide a protected base for rebuilding centrifuge production damaged in earlier attacks.
What is inside and how close it is to becoming operational remain publicly unverified. Satellite photographs show continued construction and reinforced entrances.

An assessment in September by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (a thinktank based in the US) found an increased level of activity at Pickaxe Mountain during 2026. Analysts have not been able to confirm that centrifuges have been moved there, however.

Calls for nuclear weapons and a nuclear test in Iranian media and political circles, alongside speculation about Mojtaba Khamenei’s willingness to approve a shift towards nuclear deterrence, have added to concerns about the site.

However, the images alone cannot establish that enrichment or bomb making is happening inside. International inspectors have never been given access, leaving the interior’s layout and contents publicly unverified.
Why is it difficult to attack?

The protection for the new facility comes from the mountain itself, which is composed of dense granite. The depth of 80-100m for the complex is an estimate drawn from external evidence; detailed plans have never been published.

America’s largest conventional bunker-buster, the GBU-57, was used against Fordow and Natanz in June 2025. Its performance against Pickaxe Mountain remains uncertain. Figures describing penetration through earth tell us little about the same weapon’s performance through dense rock.

The Trump administration could try to interrupt access and operations without reaching the deepest halls. Public military assessments discuss attacks on entrances and external infrastructure. Such damage could delay work, and repeated attacks could complicate repairs. Equipment buried deeper might survive.

This creates a problem after the bombing stops. Satellite images can reveal a collapsed entrance. Establishing what happened far underground is much harder. A president could announce a successful operation while inspectors and analysts remain unable to verify its effect on Iran’s capabilities.
Could a strike give Trump an exit?

Pickaxe Mountain offers Trump a target around which he could build a victory speech. After a politically costly war, a strike would let him claim that he had dealt with Iran’s remaining nuclear threat and could bring American operations to an end: damage the facility, declare victory and withdraw.

That calculation is also being discussed inside Iran. One possible course would be to let Trump claim victory and avoid retaliation so the war could end. Claims that the Trump administration had requested such an arrangement have circulated. Iran’s foreign ministry, however, dismissed them and insisted that any attack would receive a response.

There could be an opportunity here for Tehran. If underground equipment survived and Trump accepted visible damage as grounds to leave, Iran could preserve capabilities while allowing the White House to claim success. The mountain could become a useful lure.

Yet evidence that Iran has deliberately prepared such an outcome remains thin: construction began years before this confrontation. Reinforcing the site also serves the straightforward purpose of protecting it.

Even a spectacular strike would leave the confrontation over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz unresolved. The danger is that each side expects the other to stop. Trump could assume a limited attack would close the confrontation; Tehran could decide that answering it was essential to its credibility.

Meanwhile, damage visible from space would leave unanswered questions about equipment and material underground. Ending the confrontation would still require an agreement covering nuclear inspections, shipping through Hormuz, sanctions on Iran and the wider disputes keeping the conflict alive.

articles.title: New blood test claims to detect 50-plus cancers before symptoms – but there’s no evidence it can reduce your risk of dying from cancer
articles.author: Andrew Wolf, Professor Emeritus of Medicine, University of Virginia
paras: Cancer isn’t the leading cause of death in the United States; heart disease ranks first in that regard. But it’s cancer that strikes fear into the hearts of many Americans.

Cancer can take an excruciating toll on its millions of victims and their family members. Cancer treatments are often highly toxic, and the disease is increasingly striking people at younger ages, which is why it accounts for more years of potential life lost than heart disease.

So when a blood test comes along that claims to be able to screen for over 50 cancers at once in a single blood draw before symptoms appear – as is the case for the Galleri test, by the biotech company GRAIL – it might seem like society has a Holy Grail of modern medicine at their fingertips.
But a closer look at the evidence suggests that the Galleri test is not yet the universal screening breakthrough patients and doctors hope for.
As a physician who studies early cancer detection, and as chair of the American Cancer Society’s screening guideline development group, I have been following this test’s development with interest.

While the Galleri test certainly shows great promise, clinical trial data indicates that it struggles with early-stage cancer detection and has not yet been shown to lower the risk of death from cancer or prevent advanced cancer. Across all cancer stages, the test missed over two-thirds of cancer cases.

On Sept. 23, 2026, an advisory panel to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration voted to recommend approval of the Galleri test. While a recommendation from the FDA’s advisory panel is not the same as full approval from the agency, it marks a critical first step in the process of potentially making the test widely available to the American public. The FDA has not yet announced when it will make a decision on the test.

But even as the advisory panel approved the test, panelists recommended that the word “early” be removed from “early cancer detection test” in product labeling. Panel members were not convinced the test can find cancers at their earliest and most curable stages, and they expressed uncertainty about the test’s benefit to patients at this time.
Given this uncertainty, careful scrutiny of the data behind the test can help doctors and patients make informed decisions about whether to use it.
What is the Galleri test? How does it work?

Galleri is part of an emerging class of multicancer early detection tests. These tests do not diagnose cancer: If a test is positive, further evaluation is necessary to determine whether cancer is present, and, if so, what type of cancer. It is offered as a screening test, similar to mammography for breast cancer screening or PSA testing for prostate cancer screening, but with the potential advantage of screening for many cancers at once, including many for which no screening test currently exists.

The Galleri test looks for DNA fragments in blood that are associated with cancer. When something goes wrong with your DNA, whether because you inherited a mutation or something in your environment triggered that mutation, the processes that regulate cell division can go awry. Uncontrolled cell division can trigger the growth of cancer cells.

Galleri and other multicancer early detection tests in development look for differences that distinguish the DNA produced by tumor cells from normal cells. Galleri identifies unique tags on cancer DNA called methylation markers and uses machine learning algorithms to generate a positive or negative test result.
What are the strengths of the Galleri test?

The Galleri test looks for DNA signals from over 50 cancers, including the 12 that account for almost two-thirds of cancer deaths in the U.S, such as lung and pancreas cancer. Importantly, it provides information on which organ the possible tumor likely originated from. Currently recommended cancer screenings are largely limited to four types of cancer.

Many of the cancers the Galleri test looks for are not currently included in routine screening. Moreover, the test has a very low false positive rate: Only about 0.5% of people who get the test are incorrectly identified as having cancer, or one person out of every 200 tests. A false positive rate is the percentage of people who are told they have cancer but actually don’t. This requires that patients get more testing, which can be costly, sometimes risky and often worrisome.
In comparison, many currently recommended screening tests, such as the Cologuard stool test for colorectal cancer, have false positive rates in the 10% range.

This very low false positive rate also translates into another strength – a very high positive predictive value, or PPV, which is the probability that a positive test result actually means cancer is present. The PPV of the Galleri test was 52% across three annual screens, meaning over half the positive results actually led to a cancer diagnosis. This is good because it gives people confidence that the test is more than 50% correct.

For context, the PPVs of most recommended screening tests – such as stool tests for colorectal cancer, mammography for breast cancer, or the HPV test for cervical cancer – are typically below 10%, meaning most positive results don’t lead to a cancer diagnosis.

The Galleri test also can predict with high accuracy where a cancer originated in the body. In one study of 32,000 U.S. adults age 50 and older who received a Galleri blood test, cancer was diagnosed in about 0.5% of them – 173 patients. Of these patients, the test correctly predicted the cancer type in 91%. This specificity could help clinicians select more targeted evaluations rather than looking for cancer anywhere in the body.
What are the limitations of the Galleri test?
Despite these impressive results, the Galleri test has several major shortcomings.

For one, the test is not as good at detecting cancer in its earliest stages as currently recommended screening tests, which is the main point of a cancer screening test. The test’s ability to detect cancer at all stages was less than 31% over three annual rounds of screening, meaning the test missed 69% of cases. Of the cancers detected in the study, comparing outcomes from getting the Galleri test three years in a row to routine cancer screening, 60% of the cancers detected in the people who got the Galleri test were early stage, which was almost identical to those who didn’t get it.

In addition, the Galleri test did not perform any better than standard screening tests at detecting cancer early. The detection rate for early-stage cancers was only 21% over three years of screening, meaning almost 80% were missed. Cancer is most curable in its early stages, so this shortcoming is a major one. Such a low detection rate can lead to false reassurance from an incorrectly negative test result.

Perhaps the most important shortcoming of the Galleri test is that it hasn’t yet proved that it can save lives or even reduce the risk of being diagnosed with late-stage cancer. The main goal of the trial was to show that the test could reduce the incidence of late-stage cancers over three years of screening – and it failed to do so. In other words, one of the hopes was that the test could reduce the risk of being diagnosed with advanced cancer by finding and treating cancer early – but as of now, there is no evidence to support this.

There was a hint that the incidence of Stage 4 cancer was trending lower by the third year of screening. But more time is needed to determine whether this is a true finding and, if so, whether it leads to a lower risk of dying from cancer.
Requests for comment from GRAIL were not returned.
What did the FDA’s panel recommend?
The FDA advisory panel took three votes. While one of of these votes followed the evidence, two of them were surprisingly counterintuitive.

First, the panel voted 10-0 to recommend that the Galleri test is safe. While undergoing a blood test doesn’t typically involve any substantive risk, a positive result may prompt further testing, such as biopsies, that are riskier than a blood test and can incur additional costs.

These harms can be particularly hard to swallow if the test turns out to be a false alarm, as it will in about half of cases. One study evaluating Galleri’s safety found that 0.6% of those who had the test ended up undergoing an invasive diagnostic procedure, but none experienced serious complications. Hence, the safety vote appears to have been warranted.

Second, the panel voted 6-4 to recommend that the test is effective, though a number of the panelists cast their yes vote on the condition that the company remove the term “early” from the label “multi-cancer early detection” test.

This outcome, however, does not have the evidence to back it up. Available studies indicate the Galleri test does not reduce the incidence of late-stage cancer and performs poorly in detecting early-stage cancer. Additionally, there is no evidence that it lowers the risk of dying from cancer.

Finally, the panel voted 7-2 with one abstention to recommend that the benefits of the Galleri test outweigh the risk. But if there is no proven benefit to the test, how can the benefits outweigh the risks, even if the risk is low?

While the advisory panel acknowledged the test’s serious limitations, it still went ahead and recommended approval. One of the panel members stated that the ability to find more early-stage cancers in a broader population is a benefit, even though that hasn’t been proved yet. “So perhaps my ‘yes’ is a hopeful (vote) rather than an accurate one,” said the panel member.
The problem is that “hope” does not reduce death and disability from cancer.
Should you get the Galleri test or not?

If the FDA agrees with its advisory panel’s recommendation and approves the Galleri test, it will likely be more widely marketed to the American public. Regardless, there remain many caveats, and I believe patients will want to be cautious.

First, FDA approval does not guarantee insurance coverage. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has a separate coverage determination process, and it is not required to grant coverage to FDA-approved tests. The out-of-pocket cost of the Galleri test is currently US$949.

It remains unclear whether the test can reduce your risk of dying from cancer or being diagnosed with advanced cancer. However, if you’re willing to pay the annual cost of the test, are willing to undergo further testing despite a high rate of false alarms, and are not overly reassured by a falsely negative test result, you can ask your doctor for more information about the test.

What doctors and researchers are certain about is the importance of staying up to date with currently recommended cancer screening tests for colon, breast, cervical and lung cancers, even if you decide to get the Galleri test. These tests are proven to detect early-stage cancer and lower your risk of dying from cancer. That’s the bottom line.

Andrew Wolf serves as Chair of the American Cancer Society's Guideline Development Group. This is a volunteer position. Opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the American Cancer Society.

articles.title: I’m an artist who works with glass – here’s how the physics and chemistry of glassblowing work
articles.author: Suzanne Peck, Lecturer of Art, Rochester Institute of Technology
paras: Glass as a material is full of contradictions. Depending on the form and use, glass can be fragile or strong, opaque or transparent, rough or smooth. The studios my colleagues and I teach and learn in, as glass instructors, echo this abundance of physical opposites. These environments are simultaneously immersive, complex, seductive and demanding.

When the studio is in action, you might hear glass breaking, hot metal being quenched in water, glassblowing pipes rolling on the workbench rails, and some good tunes on the stereo. You might smell hot beeswax and burning newspaper. You might feel a bit of waste glass under your shoe or the intense heat from the furnaces and a breeze from a well-placed fan. Glassblowers learn to listen, to feel and to find some focus within and among the kinetic.

The constant stimuli of the glass studio may not seem anything like a sterile science lab, and yet glass artists need to accrue knowledge of physics and chemistry to achieve any kind of control with this dynamic material. They must choose a material with the desired properties and during the process judge factors such as heat and malleability.

At Rochester Institute of Technology, where I help run the glass program, we primarily use two types of glasses. In our hot glass studio we melt “soft” glass. This glass is specifically formulated to be melted in a furnace and used by the glassblower. It’s a combination of fine mesh silica sand, soda ash and lime, with small amounts of a few additional ingredients that keep the glass beautiful when it’s at its top temperature of 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit (1,204 degrees Celsius).

In our flameworking studio, we use a borosilicate glass. You might recognize this glass as the brand Pyrex made in Corning, New York. This is a super heat-resistant glass. It melts at a higher temperature than soft glass and arrives to our students in preformed rods that they can melt and shape by torch in our flameworking studio. The differences in chemistry really change how these glasses look and behave.

Glass, from a material science perspective, is categorized as an amorphous solid, meaning that glass’s molecules are arranged in a near-random pattern and there is no sharp melting point. Rather, glass gradually softens over a wide temperature range.
Once you’ve adjusted to the chaos of the studio, it’s time to start working.

We have two furnaces in our hot glass studio, where we work with soft glass, so anytime during the school year there is between 700 to 1,200 pounds of glass. It’s kept in the furnace at its molten state (2,200 degrees F or 1,204 degrees C), ready to be gathered and transformed.

When we work with the material, transforming it with tools and breath and heat, it needs to be kept in a workable heat zone – probably between 1,100 and 2,000 F (593 and 1,094 C). When the glass dips below that range, we perceive it as solid, though at the molecular level it is still dynamic and acting more like a liquid.

To make anything – a sculpture, a tumbler, a celestial magical orb or a pumpkin – you start by gathering glass out of the furnace on a metal rod. Once you’ve gathered your glass, you start making decisions.

You might ask yourself: What tools do I need to begin to shape and transform this glass into the object I have in mind? If you wait too long and the glass begins cooling down, you’ll need to reheat it to reintroduce malleability, allowing you to continue working it without breaking it.

A big part of glasswork is moving between the reheating chamber and the bench, where the artist uses tools to move and stretch the molten glass into the desired shape. You’ll need to alternate between these two stations many times.

Glassblowing is a team activity. I have physical and intellectual support from my colleagues: breath from their lungs, protection from the heat, additional bits of glass brought from the furnace to add to my object. We almost never work alone.

So, say I want to make a very basic clear tumbler. This is a simple conceptual object – utilitarian, domestic and intimate. It is also a tricky one to make well: too heavy and it feels bad in the hand, too thick at the lip and it dribbles when you drink, too thin at the bottom and it will break before it is complete.

Maybe I want to design it so it is slightly conical: wider at the bottom than the top, so it’s less likely to tip over. Maybe I want it to have a little indent for the user’s thumb as a gentle invitation to her hand. First I make my design: I draw it. I share it with my team so they can predict the process and the object’s needs. Then we begin.

I gather glass out of the furnace, let it cool a bit, then introduce a bubble in the glass by blowing into the pipe, the hollow rod that attaches to the object I’m making. I reheat, sit at the bench and begin to shape the glass using both gravity and the Jills, a cooling and shaping tool. The Jills is kind of like a large pair of tongs. It hasn’t changed much in design for 2,000 years.

I ask for some air from my teammate, and she blows into the pipe while I’m shaping the glass. The bubble transforms into a pill shape, slightly wider at the bottom. I constrict the area right in front of the pipe. I’m focusing on shape and heat, taking care to not let the glass get too cold. If the glass drops to about 1,000 F (538 C), it enters a danger zone. If it’s not yet finished, it needs to be warmed up in the reheating chamber; or if it is done, put away in a kiln to cool slowly.

If glass cools too quickly, the molecules freeze into a chaotic pattern, which causes stresses that result in fracture. To combat this volatility, when the glass object is done and ready to be cooled, we place the object in an annealer: a kiln set to a resting temperature of 930 F (500 C).

This temperature is like a Goldilocks zone for our glass: It’s not so hot that the glass will deform, but not so cool that the glass will stress and break. Once the kilns are full, a computer guide takes them down to room temperature over about 10 hours.

As I continue to work on my cup, I get more heat, focusing on the very end of the bubble – the part that will be the base of the cup. I then sit down and have another member of my team flatten the bottom with a wooden paddle while I tool the glass with the Jills to keep its shape. The cycle continues on and on.

The process is quick, but also there are so many little steps that it would take nearly a full-length book to describe them all. When asked how long it takes to make a tumbler, I’ll often answer, “About 10 years or 10 minutes, depending on how you think about time and material knowledge.” This is both glib and true. Glass demands attention, dedication and a willingness to make connections between physics and chemistry and your observable experiences. It is a highly challenging and equally rewarding material to work with and alongside. I count myself very lucky.

articles.title: Why do farts smell so bad? A microbiologist explains the odors brewing in your gut
articles.author: Brenda A. Wilson, Professor of Microbiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why do farts smell so bad? – Daisy, age 7, New York, New York
A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. All together, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an important job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

As a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.
So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?
Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

Anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

But wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

One key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

Only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.
Your gut’s source of grody gases
The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.
However, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

When you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

As you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

Farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness book of world records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mis-hears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

But sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves and volcano vents that can suffocate and kill you.
So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

articles.title: Archaeological finds at an Irish fort reveal insights into the finer side of medieval life
articles.author: Michelle Comber, Lecturer in Archaeology, School of Geography, Archaeology and Irish Studies, University of Galway
paras: Popular media, from computer games to movies, often portrays medieval life as being dominated by fighters and farmers. In these depictions, there’s little evidence of a world beyond political struggle and simple subsistence.

Leisure activities are often overlooked, despite the fact that they existed in one form or another at most – if not all – levels of medieval society. The intangible nature of much of the evidence, often coupled with poor preservation of physical objects, can help explain this.

However, when conditions are right, archaeological remains can shed light on the extra-curricular activities of medieval folk. My colleagues and I found abundant evidence of life’s luxuries at the site of Caherconnell Cashel in the Burren region of western Ireland.

Caherconnell Cashel was a farmstead of houses and workshops enclosed within a well-preserved circular dry stone wall. Such settlements are also known as ringforts and generally housed a single family (possibly multiple generations). Caherconnell was a large ringfort; the home of wealthy local rulers from the late 10th century AD to the early 17th century. Our recently concluded excavations revealed all aspects of life at this well-preserved family settlement.

While activities such as fighting, farming, industry and crafts were clearly represented in material recovered from the site, so too were the less mundane activities of game playing, literacy, and music.

The true extent of game playing is undoubtedly lost in the perishable nature of the materials used extensively in such pursuits – such as wood, leather and textiles. At Caherconnell, however, surviving evidence includes small gaming pieces made of bone and antler, metal, clay and stone.

One of the more complete finds was an 11th-century barrel-shaped and polished antler gaming piece. A bronze peg or stem runs through its hollow core and projects from its base. It originally had a plate or cap at the top, the loss of which may have resulted in the piece being discarded or set aside for repair.

Pegged game pieces like this were used in the Saxon and Viking board game of hnefatafl, a game that appeared in Ireland around the 9th or 10th century AD. Hnefatafl, and other games like it, provided both strategy training and entertainment.

Evidence of literacy at Caherconnell includes writing implements and associated equipment. One of our most remarkable finds was an 11th-century pen made from bone and bronze. The slender hollow bone shaft or barrel was probably made from the bone of a wader bird or swan.

Experimental work by the archaeologist Adam Parsons found that the closest match was a swan radius (a tubular bone) from the right-side wing. Inserted into the narrow end of the barrel is a tapering bronze point or nib.

The Caherconnell pen finds no exact comparisons within Ireland or elsewhere; its early secular context is also, so far, unique. Until now, evidence of early literacy in Ireland has been largely confined to monastic and related church sites. At Caherconnell, the pen may have been used in general record keeping and external communications.

However, it also reminds us that literate occupants of Caherconnell Cashel may have enjoyed composing, reading, and sharing ancestral pedigrees, praise poetry and epic tales “of gods and fighting men”.
The musical sounds of a settlement are rarely represented in its archaeological record. Wood, a common material in the construction of various instruments, rarely survives to the present day.

Metal and bone fittings, however, have been found during excavations, including at Caherconnell, where bone and bronze tuning pegs were among the finds. Two of the tuning pegs are readily identifiable as components of stringed instruments.

They have a circular sectioned shaft that splays slightly into a rectangular sectioned turning block at one end (now missing from the larger bone example). The opposite end pinches in slightly and is perforated by a small circular hole through which the string was attached.
The bone tuning peg, being a relatively soft material, still bears impressions from the wire-string of the instrument. Both date to the 11th century, but they are clearly from different instruments.
One had strong bronze pegs, the other had larger bone versions. Outside Ireland, shorter tuning pegs are commonly associated with lyres, lutes and fiddles (up to 65mm is classed as short).

No lutes or fiddles survive from early Ireland, however. Nor are there any written references to, or depictions of them. The lyre, on the other hand, is represented. Depictions are found in several ecclesiastical contexts and early Irish literature confirms that lyres or lyre-like instruments were also used outside religious settings.

Music, and accompanying songs and poetry, probably fulfilled various social, political, and cultural functions. These range from proclaiming the magnificence of the nobility to entertaining a family around their hearth in the evening.

Life at Caherconnell was, in many ways, very traditional. It was a place where ancestry and heritage were valued, yet it was also a place connected to the outside world. In leisure, as in so many other facets of their lives, the occupants encountered, adopted, and no doubt adapted the most desirable elements of a wider cultural realm.

It is clear from this one site that those with more leisure time, often the wealthier in society, filled that time with various recreational pursuits. However, human nature suggests that all classes engaged in such activities, albeit often in a manner that’s less visible to archaeologists.

After all, you didn’t need a fancy bronze and antler game set to play games, writing equipment to create stories, or peg-tuned wired instruments to compose and sing a song. Such things just prove the existence of these activities, not how commonplace they were.

The Caherconnell excavations were funded by the Caherconnell Archaeology Field School, and some of its post-excavation analyses by Ireland's National Monuments Service via a Royal Irish Academy research-excavation grant.

articles.title: Flesh-eating screwworm is spreading in the US, threatening livestock and wildlife – hunters can be the first line of defense
articles.author: Jacob Dykes, Assistant Professor of Wildlife Management, Mississippi State University
paras: For the first time in over 50 years, an infestation of the flesh-eating fly known as the New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) is spreading on the U.S. mainland, and it is putting livestock and other animals at risk.
The New World screwworm doesn’t just attack cattle. All warm-blooded animals are susceptible, including deer and elk, as well as small game, waterfowl and pets.
That means hunters headed to the field this fall may be the most important line of defense for spotting this destructive parasite and keeping it from spreading further.

As co-directors of the Mississippi State University deer lab, we believe the country’s millions of hunters can serve as a powerful early warning system by keeping a close eye on the state of wildlife they see. Wildlife agencies are already asking them to be vigilant and report any signs of screwworm infestations.
The problem with screwworm

Unlike other blowflies, New World screwworm larvae feed on living tissue rather than dead tissue. They lay eggs in open wounds or mucosal openings, such as the eyes and nose of livestock, deer or elk.

Wounds as small as tick bites or scratches, as well as natural openings such as the umbilical stump on newborns or on deer’s pedicles, where their antlers grow and are shed, can attract these parasites.
Once the eggs hatch, the maggots burrow into the animal’s flesh and feed, enlarging the wound and attracting more flies. Over time, this leads to infection and death.
How the US eradicated screwworm in the past
All warm-blooded animals are susceptible to the New World screwworm, but America has seen firsthand the harm they can cause to livestock.
In the 1950s, livestock producers in the U.S. Southwest lost up to US$100 million annually to New World screwworm infections, equivalent to over $1 billion today.

The nation was eventually able to eradicate the New World screwworm from the mainland in 1966 using a combination of treating infected animals and raising hundreds of millions of sterilized male flies and releasing them in infested areas.

The New World screwworm has a life cycle of only about 21 days, and each female mates only once. Because of that, inundating areas with sterile male flies for a few months, which equates to a few generations of flies, can eradicate a screwworm population.

Over time, sterile flies were used to push the New World screwworm further south, where they had been contained behind the Darién Gap, Panama’s narrow border region with Colombia. Sterile flies kept the parasite south of Panama for years, but the movement of cattle and wildlife likely brought it north again. Since 2022, the parasites have been reproducing and moving farther northward. There have been hundreds of detections in Mexico and now in the U.S.
The Florida Key deer infestation

Wildlife have received far less attention than livestock during screwworm infestations, with one exception: In July 2016, the New World screwworm was detected in the Florida Keys in an endangered deer population: the Florida Key deer (Odocoileus virginianus clavium).

At the time, the Florida Key deer population was estimated at only about 800 to 1,000 individuals. Because they were endangered and isolated, primarily on the islands of Big Pine Key and No Name Key, they were monitored more closely than most wildlife.

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists established quarantine zones. They inspected more than 16,900 animals – dogs, cats, a pig and a raccoon were also found with larvae – and they released 150 million sterile flies across the area. The islands lost 9% to 20% of the total Key Deer population, but the New World screwworm was declared eradicated there on March 23, 2017, less than a year after it was discovered.

In June 2026, screwworm was back in the United States. A rancher discovered the first New World screwworm case in a calf near La Pryor, Texas. A few more cases were confirmed in livestock and domestic animals in Texas and New Mexico.

The number of cases in animals had passed 125 as of Nov. 10, 2026, including in two elk reported by hunters in Texas. The U.S. government has started ramping up production of sterile flies to try to keep the parasites from spreading.
Although there have been only a couple of cases reported in wildlife, that isn’t necessarily reassuring.

Wildlife are far more likely to carry the parasite without being detected. Once the screwworm is detected, treatment would also be much more complicated for wildlife than for livestock, because wildlife cannot be treated individually and thus are more dependent on the use of sterile flies to eradicate screwworm.
For this reason, quickly identifying areas with New World screwworm and targeting those areas by releasing sterile flies would be more important than ever.
Tapping an army of conservationists: Hunters
Fortunately, there is an army of conservationists across the country who spend much of their time afield. These conservationists are also known as hunters.

According to the latest U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation, nearly 11.5 million hunters pursue big game and spend part of the fall and winter in the field hunting ungulate species such as deer and elk.

White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) hunters alone are expected to harvest about 6 million deer during the 2026-27 season and will observe millions more. Hunters also review tens of millions of wildlife pictures collected each year by game cameras used for scouting.

That level of surveillance can’t be matched. New Mexico’s Department of Agriculture has already called on hunters to report any suspicious larvae, particularly in Grant and Otero counties, where screwworm has been found in livestock. Hunters of all kinds, everywhere, can help.
What to watch for as a hunter
If you’re a hunter, be on the lookout for wounded animals, especially those with visible maggots, and for unusual behaviors such as restlessness, lethargy, or biting or licking wounds.

Do not move harvested animals from the field if they show signs of a New World screwworm infection. Doing so could further spread the parasite. Instead, contact the area’s state wildlife agency, the U.S. Department of Agriculture office or a local veterinarian immediately.
As hunting seasons get underway across the country, an army of conservationists will be in the field, and they have an important role to play in detecting and managing screwworm’s spread.

Hunters already contribute to conservation through license fees, excise taxes and keeping wildlife populations at healthy densities. In the face of New World screwworm, their observations may be most valuable for protecting livestock.
This article, originally published Nov. 6, 2026, has been updated with a rising number of cases.

articles.title: The hidden ways insects support animal life – from habitat to health – go way beyond being food
articles.author: Eliza Grames, Assistant Professor of Biological Sciences, Binghamton University, State University of New York
paras: There are at least 14 million insect species on Earth, and they play highly diverse roles in sustaining the natural world. Insects provide many well-known benefits – what scientists often call “ecosystem services.” For example, you can thank a bee or a hoverfly for pollinating wildflowers and agricultural crops, or credit dung beetles for decomposing manure and other waste materials.

Reports of rapid declines in insect abundance and biomass over the past decade have raised concerns about potential reductions in pollination, decomposition and other insect-provided services. Researchers have also noted that declines in insects could mean a change in the food supply for insectivores such as birds and bats.

In response to these concerns, a working group emerged as part of a Research Coordination Network on the Status of Insects, funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation. This international group of 21 researchers, including us, met via Zoom for a year and a half to discuss what declines in insects might mean for vertebrates – from birds to bats to bilbies.
What emerged from those discussions was a clear picture – insects are so much more than just food, and vertebrates rely on insects for everything from habitats to protection to health.
Insects can be ecosystem engineers, meaning they create and maintain habitats for other species.

Termites and ants build massive structures below and above ground that are used by many other species. Termite nests, for example, serve as climate-controlled spots for reptiles to lay eggs and for parrots to nest. In dry regions, some frogs live inside ant nests to take advantage of the humid conditions, masking themselves in pheromones to evade detection by their ant hosts.

The soil surrounding termite mounds also provides good conditions for species such as naked mole rats and aardvarks to make their burrows. Ant nests concentrate nutrients that enhance plant growth, thereby creating good grazing habitat for species like gazelles.
Insects protect other species
You probably don’t usually think of something as small as a beetle as a protector, or of a wasp as a bodyguard. But vertebrates rely on insects for defense, even against other vertebrates.

For example, horned lizards turn chemicals from ants into a toxic, blood-spurting defense to ward off predators such as big cats. Poisonous frogs similarly get their toxicity from the chemical compounds found in insects they eat, as do some birds and snakes, which store toxins from ants and beetles as part of their defensive strategy.

Many birds will deliberately nest near wasp nests so the threat of being stung deters potential predators. Some vertebrates even mimic insects to avoid getting eaten, such as young songbirds in the Amazon that move their heads to look like fuzzy caterpillars – which they resemble – when predators are nearby.
Insects clean and sanitize

Many insects, not just dung beetles, remove waste from ecosystems. By decomposing carcasses and dung, insects likely reduce disease transmission among wild vertebrates. For example, by tunneling through and burying dung, they make it an unsuitable place for parasites to live.

Certain mosquito species have gotten a bad reputation for transmitting diseases, including malaria, but other insects help control their populations. In their larval stage, dragonflies are fierce aquatic predators that eat mosquito larvae.

The ability of insects to spread diseases has even led to conservation success stories. In Australia, when native marsupials such as bilbies were threatened by invasive European rabbits, scientists used mosquitoes to transmit a virus that helped control rabbit populations. This effort resulted in populations of bilbies and other native marsupials rebounding.

Researchers have also discovered hundreds of medicinal compounds in insects, and there are likely many more to be found. For instance, chimpanzees will press flying insects into wounds, suggesting that they may have a medicinal effect, though people don’t yet know the exact insect species the chimps use.
Insects provide food for other species

Of course, insects are really important food supplies. In terms of sheer numbers and biomass, they dominate nearly every terrestrial and freshwater ecosystem. If you added up the weight of all the insects on Earth, they would vastly outweigh all the wild vertebrates and be on par with the total weight of humans and livestock combined.
It is no wonder vertebrates eat a tremendous number of insects, and this is true not just of songbirds and bats but even grizzly bears, which eat moths to help bulk up for the winter.

Perhaps even more important are all the many indirect effects insects have on the food supply. Small wasps are the only pollinators of fig trees, which provide fruit to over 1,200 vertebrate species. Many other plants also rely on insects as pollinators and have for millions of years, and vertebrates in turn rely on the seeds and fruit those plants produce.

Changes in insect communities can also have big impacts on interactions between vertebrates. When an invasive ant disrupted the mutual relationship between a native ant species and an acacia bush, it led more elephants to eat the acacia. The loss of bushes made it harder for lions to ambush zebras, their primary prey, and resulted in a shift toward lions hunting more buffalo, altering the wider ecosystem.

Another fascinating example are sloths and their moths. For a long time, it was a bit of a mystery why sloths would make the slow and dangerous journey to the ground to defecate once a week. As it turns out, sloths host a moth species that lives in their fur. The moths provide nutrients to the algae that grows in the sloth fur, which the sloth then eats. The algae also gives sloths a green tinge that helps camouflage them in the forest. The moths reproduce in sloth dung, and thus the sloth returning to the ground allows the moths to complete their life cycle.
The importance of insect conservation

Insect conservation is critical to the future of biodiversity. Insects fill so many roles and perform so many services for human beings and other species, including charismatic vertebrates people know and love, such as sloths and songbirds. As a result, declines in insect abundance and biomass could ripple out and destabilize ecosystems.

The examples we brought together in our paper in the journal Nature Reviews Biodiversity are just some of the insect-vertebrate relationships that exist, and there is a vast array of fascinating things that insects do, and do for us, that scientists know very little about.
By conserving insects, people are not just conserving the insects themselves but also supporting the many species, including humans, that depend on them.

articles.title: ‘I heard a barnacle’ – how paying attention to nature’s background noise can reveal animal secrets
articles.author: Phil Starks, Associate Professor of Biology, Tufts University
paras: During four days on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula, I saw an Olympic marmot, a species found nowhere else on Earth; four bumblebee species working the same lavender plant; three western hermit crab species new to me; and five orcas slicing through the dark water off Ediz Hook. Any one of them could have been the trip’s highlight.
Yet the encounter I cannot stop talking about occurred at low tide at Tongue Point, when I heard a barnacle.
While I had seen thousands of barnacles, I had never imagined I could hear one. It made a noise that sounded like: Clickety-clack. Clickety-clack. Pop.

As a professor who teaches about animal behavior, I know that the distinction between encountering an animal and actually noticing what it is doing is one of the simplest ways into natural history. It requires no laboratory and, at first, no special expertise.
Mostly it requires learning how to let something ordinary become interesting again.
My habit in places like a rocky shore is to become still and let my vision soften. Instead of staring at one point, I allow movement anywhere in the visual field to pull my attention.

At Tongue Point, I was thinking about the demands of life in the intertidal zone, the shore between high and low tide: temperature swings, desiccation and the cost of remaining clamped shut in open air. Then I noticed the soundscape.

At first, the clicking was just coastal noise. I attributed it to small shore crabs moving among the mussels, or hermit crab shells knocking against them. Then one sharp pop pulled my attention to a single acorn barnacle. Its tiny opening was slightly unsealed, and two small plates were moving against its deeply ridged shell. The movement appeared to coincide with another pop. Then another.
The repetition gave me something to follow. You can train yourself to do this almost anywhere.

When I take students or my sons to watch honeybees, I tell them not to stare directly at the hive entrance. Instead, sit nearby, look toward the open sky, and relax your gaze. At first you see empty air. Then a bee crosses it. Then another. Within moments the emptiness becomes a busy airport of arrivals and departures.
Nothing new has entered the scene. You have just changed what you are capable of noticing.

Observation has its own traps. Sometimes you can miss behavior because it blends into the background. Other times you see something perfectly but stop asking questions because somebody has already told you what it means.

Orb-weaver spiders offer a good example. Some add conspicuous bands or patches of dense silk to their webs. These structures are called stabilimenta, a name inherited from the old idea that they stabilize or strengthen the web. But they don’t.

Researchers later found evidence for several possible functions: attracting prey, deterring or confusing predators, protecting webs from larger animals, and, in some cases, helping with temperature regulation. Different functions may matter in different species, environments or stages of life.

I first became interested in the debate over stabilimentum function because I was unconvinced that one explanation could account for all the evidence. I started out asking whether somebody was wrong. The better question turned out to be why researchers expected one universal answer in the first place.

That remains one of my favorite lessons from animal behavior: A name can be useful, but it can also sneak in an explanation. Once you think you know what something is, you become less likely to watch what it actually does.
The opposite mistake is just as easy: seeing something interesting and immediately deciding you understand it.

After I returned from the Olympic Peninsula, I emailed a retired marine invertebrate zoologist and described what I had seen and heard. His response was delighted and appropriately skeptical: “Doubt it. Take a short video next time.”

I saw an open barnacle move and heard a pop at the same time. That is an observation. I did not demonstrate that the barnacle produced the sound. A mussel bed contains crabs, moving shells and a host of other possible sources. A close-up video with synchronized audio could test whether the same visible movement repeatedly coincided with each pop.
Noticing something is the start of science. It does not let you skip the work that follows.
For anyone who wants to become a better naturalist, a simple sequence helps:
Ask what else could explain it.
Decide what evidence would distinguish among those possibilities.
Try it somewhere familiar: a backyard, city park, pond edge, patch of flowers or shoreline. Stay longer than feels necessary. Let the sights and sounds become background.
Then look for repetition. One movement, then another like it. One sound that separates from the rest. An animal returning to the same place.

And once something catches your attention, resist the urge to explain it too quickly. Watch again. You may discover something genuinely unusual. More likely, you will discover something ordinary that you had never actually seen before.
I may not have witnessed rare behavior at Tongue Point or identified a rare species. But I stayed long enough to wonder what I was hearing. Maybe that was rare enough.

articles.title: AI won’t ever make a historically accurate film – but it could help archaeology create better stories
articles.author: Stephan Blum, Research Associate, Institute for Prehistory and Early History and Medieval Archaeology, University of Tübingen
paras: Tech billionaire Elon Musk was up in arms about the recent adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey by director Christopher Nolan, which he heavily criticised for its diverse casting and accused of lacking historical accuracy. Claiming he wanted to show that artificial intelligence could bypass traditional Hollywood studios and deliver a story “historically accurate and true to the art of Homer” at a fraction of the cost, he set his AI Grok Imagine to the task.
On October 23, the platform posted the first seven minutes.

As archaeologists and art historians, we’re not here to review the film for its artistic quality or even its historic accuracy. Instead, we’re here to point out the real problem with the whole endeavour: the promise of historical accuracy failed before the first frame was even rendered.

Contrary to what many of you might assume, as historians we think Musk’s underlying idea – bringing together everything archaeology and history have to offer and using AI as a tool to explore and work with that knowledge – is a genuinely exciting one. We see considerable potential in that approach: a system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar can hold in mind, such as how ceramic styles spread. The problem is turning that into a film that claims to be historically accurate.
Any attempt to produce a complete, coherent visual narrative would inevitably require AI to go beyond the evidence and invent what we do not know.

Archaeology is inevitably working with a fragmentary record: only a tiny proportion of the past survives in the ground, and only a fraction of that is ever excavated. For instance, open the boxes in the Troy depot and you’ll find spindle whorls and loom weights; however, you won’t find the cloth they made. Everyone at Troy wore textiles but the textiles are gone.

So, like the textiles, everything that cannot be recovered directly from the archaeological record has to be interpreted and explained through hypotheses, however well-founded they may be scientifically. There will always be gaps, uncertainties and competing interpretations.
AI, by design, would inevitably fill these gaps.

Suppose Grok Imagine was given everything the Troy Project holds: a century and a half of excavation, thousands of plans, pottery drawings and photographs, plus the small-finds catalogue. It would generate connections, details and entire scenarios where the historical and archaeological evidence offers no firm answers.
Generative AI is built to produce complete images, even when there are visible gaps. These gaps are often filled with influence from other existing media like film sets, games, paintings.

This is precisely where the problem lies: additions by AI may be plausible, even convincing. Some sceptical reviewers concede that some of those seven minutes pass for real. But convincing is not accurate, and the space between the two is where archaeology lives.

The Odyssey is also an interesting target for accuracy. It’s a poor witness to the past: shaped centuries after the palaces its about fell, it is a palimpsest of Mycenaean memory and iron age worldview – not a snapshot. Odysseus, Helen and Circe are not people archaeology could confirm. However, there is a lot of creative media about the world these characters are believed to have inhabited.

Back to those textiles. A model trained on that record would inherit our ignorance along with our knowledge. It will hallucinate or imagine because it must paint every pixel. It will draw on all the evidence, media and more connected to the themes and history to render a finished cloak, dyed and draped. This rendering will look like a convincingly accurate garment where the honest research answer is “fibre known, colour unknown”.
What survives is not what happened

None of this makes AI useless. A system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar could see – such as how ceramic styles spread. But every such pattern would first be a pattern in the record, not a picture of the past.

A genuinely archaeological AI would do what generative AI rarely does: show its uncertainty as clearly as its confidence. Take armour. Only fragments survive at Troy. Where evidence permits several reconstructions, it would show several rather than present one confident, definitive option. Where only fragments survive, it would show only the fragments. And where the evidence runs out, it would say so, clearly marking what is documented, what is inferred and what is merely plausible.

This approach to rendering possibilities is close to what the London Charter (2009) and the Seville Principles (2011), two international guidelines for virtual reconstructions of heritage, have long demanded: transparency rather than smoothing.

Which world gets reconstructed is also a choice. Troy spans phases centuries apart, and Mycenaean palaces differed from Hittite cities: there is no single “bronze age”. The record can support a conflict at Troy; it cannot establish Homer’s Trojan war as one event. However, an AI model picks one Troy and never mentions the choice.

The film will likely be forgotten within a news cycle or two; what remains is the method. The most accurate Odyssey would not be the most definitive or confident one; it would end where we began: on the boxes of whorls and weights, and the empty space where the cloth should be.
Historical accuracy does not mean filling every gap. It means showing where the gaps are.

articles.title: AI could transform mathematics, but humans will still need to be in the loop
articles.author: Carolin Antos, Assistant Professor of Philosophy, University of Konstanz
paras: OpenAI recently announced that one of its AI models solved one of the hardest problems in modern mathematics: the Navier–Stokes problem. The equations at the heart of this problem describe the movement of fluids like water and, according to the scientific definition, air.

The Navier-Stokes equations are essential to understanding phenomena such as ocean currents, blood circulation, and airflow over airplane wings. Yet, mathematicians have struggled for decades to determine whether coherent solutions to these equations exist.

It was for this reason that the US-based Clay Mathematics Institute, which is dedicated to disseminating mathematical knowledge, chose the Navier-Stokes problem as one of its seven Millennium Prize Problems.

These are the most important and challenging unsolved problems in modern mathematics, with a prize of US$1 million (£746,000; €895,000) offered for the first correct solution to each. A problem that resisted generations of mathematicians thus has apparently been solved by artificial intelligence.

While these advancements sent shock waves through the mathematical world, they seem to be only the tip of the iceberg: On October 6 2026, OpenAI presented its solutions to more than 300 longstanding unsolved problems across most areas of mathematics with their new internal model.

Does this mark the end of mathematics as a human endeavour? Answering this question requires a closer look at mathematical proofs. Broadly speaking, a proof is an argument for a mathematical claim that starts from generally accepted assumptions and proceeds through the different steps of reasoning for the claim.

Before mathematicians accept such an argument as a proof, they need to check that each step is correct. Computers can increasingly help with this task, but for major AI-generated results, human mathematical supervision and expertise remains indispensable.

However, a fully verified proof is not the end of the story. Mathematicians do not only want to know that a theorem is true; they also want to understand why it is true and what can be learned from its proof.

Professor Terence Tao, from Unversity of California, Los Angeles, is one of the world’s leading mathematicians and a prominent supporter of AI’s use in mathematics. He recently coined the term “proof digestion” for the many ways that mathematicians continue to work with a proof after its correctness has been established.

They may reorganise the proof around more natural concepts, streamline a complicated argument, connect it to existing mathematics, or extract methods that can be applied elsewhere. Proof digestion itself can be highly fruitful and produce new mathematics.

Even after a proof has been digested, the mathematical work is rarely done. Major mathematical results often become stepping stones towards new open problems. Important variants of the Navier-Stokes problem, for example, cannot be solved by the methods of the recent proof proposed by OpenAI. This is typical of major breakthroughs: their importance often lies not only in answering a long-standing question, but also in introducing novel mathematical concepts and opening up new lines of research.

Often, one proof simply is not enough. Mathematicians regularly search for new proofs of results that have already been proven. Take, for example, the Pythagorean Theorem: a² +b² = c². This relates to the three lengths of a right-angled triangle.

This result was proved in antiquity, yet a book published in the 1920s collects more than 300 proofs for the Pythagorean Theorem that have been established over the last two millennia. If the only purpose of a proof is to establish that a result is true, all but the earliest of these proofs would be redundant.

Instead, the opposite is the case: different proofs may reveal new insights into why the result is true, uncover new connections to concepts from other mathematical areas, or suggest new methods of generalisation. Thus, proofs are not only valued for verifying mathematical results, but also for the explanation and understanding they provide.

What exactly makes a proof explanatory or illuminating is difficult to pin down – and remains an ongoing topic in the philosophy of mathematics. This makes explanation and understanding much less clear goals for AI than simply producing a correct proof.

The recent advancements in AI will likely transform mathematical practice profoundly. But mathematics is not simply the production of correct answers to unsolved problems. Proofs still need to be understood, reorganised, connected to other results and used to generate new questions.

As AI models become ever more effective at producing proofs, these other parts of mathematical research may become increasingly important. In the near future, it may therefore matter less who – or what – can produce a proof, than whether this can be used for mathematical progress.
