articles.title: Why do blind people and musicians hear pitch better? New research suggests they have less internal noise
articles.author: Woon Ju Park, Assistant Professor of Psychology, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: People who have lived most of their lives blind often have extraordinary hearing abilities. In new research published in the Journal of Neuroscience, my colleagues and I discovered that this ability arises from how their auditory systems are able to more consistently and reliably process sounds compared with people who aren’t blind. And interestingly, sighted musicians seem to enhance their hearing through a similar mechanism.
Hearing is a complicated process. It involves many stages, starting from how the ears detect sounds and going all the way up to how the brain extracts meaningful information from those sounds.

Different mechanisms are involved, too. You can get better at hearing by being more selective or more consistent. Think of writing the letter “A.” You can practice to make your “A” either more distinguishable from “B” or look more similar to other “A’s” every time you write it. The latter is called internal noise – how consistently your auditory system responds to the same sound over time. The less internal noise you have, the more reliably you can tell similar sounds apart.

We recruited nine individuals who became blind before the age of 2 and 18 sighted individuals. Participants in both groups had varying levels of musical training, giving us an opportunity to examine how musical experience can also affect hearing abilities.

Participants completed two simple hearing tasks. In one task, they detected a tone presented in background noise, which allowed us to assess how the cochlea in the inner ear processes different sound frequencies. In the other task, they judged which of the two tones had a higher pitch, a task that also relies on how the brain interprets sound information.

We found that people with early-life blindness were better than sighted people only in the pitch discrimination task. This means that their improved hearing abilities may selectively originate from changes in how their brains process auditory information and not from how their ears detect sounds.

Importantly, we used a mathematical model to better understand what drives differences in pitch discrimination. The model showed that the enhanced ability to tell pitches apart in people with early-life blindness happens by reducing internal noise: more consistent and reliable processing of sounds rather than greater selectivity for different sound frequencies.

Surprisingly, we found that musical training seems to similarly reduce internal noise. Sighted musicians also responded to sounds more consistently compared with people who neither experienced early-life blindness nor received extensive musical training.
Because your brain doesn’t know what kind of sensory environment it’ll encounter when you’re born, it’s equipped with a special ability: to tune its responses to parts of the world that matter to it.

This ability helps people see, hear and master new skills as their experiences change, like when children learn to read and when adults learn to identify different bird species. Words and birds have become a meaningful part of their experiences, so their brains are tuned to the new information.

Our study identifies internal noise as an important factor that facilitates this brain plasticity. There are many ways a person can come to have reduced levels of internal noise, and one is by building a more accurate template for perceiving the world.
It is possible that sensory experience, whether it be being blind or being a musician, might help create and fine-tune the perceptual template relevant for hearing.

If sensory experiences and training can tap into the brain’s ability to adapt, researchers may be able to use them to improve perceptual abilities. For example, targeted training to hear sound locations could help people who are beginning to lose vision learn to rely on other senses to navigate.
However, researchers still don’t know how much training is needed and what aspects of the auditory experience are key to drive behaviorally meaningful changes in the brain.

Another important question is whether and how this brain plasticity varies depending on when someone loses their vision or begins musical training. The brain might have greater plasticity early in development, and how sensory experiences shape the brain may differ in adulthood.

How far can people push their ability to learn? Can everyone become super listeners with training? If the brain’s plasticity is limited in adulthood, are there ways to reopen the door? And what role does internal noise play in this learning?

Moving forward, our team is interested in understanding whether the enhanced pitch discrimination we saw in people with early-life blindness and sighted musicians extends to more complex, everyday listening.

articles.title: AI agents with friendly faces and adorable bodies can distract you from serious risks
articles.author: Ankolika De, Postdoctoral fellow, Vanderbilt University
paras: Meta’s Muse is a personal artificial intelligence agent that sends email for you, shops and books travel for you, and uses your apps to act on your behalf. When you call on it from your phone or computer, a little avatar named Jolly appears, looking something like a digitized teddy bear that blinks and waves to you.

Meta also released Muse Charm, a device with a screen the size of a flattened golf ball that you can keep in your pocket so you can access Jolly anytime. Journalists have described Muse as “magical” and “cutesy.” They have compared Charm to a Tamagotchi, a handheld digital pet that you hatched from an egg and guided through baby, child, teen and adult stages, that was all the rage in the 1990s.

Right on Muse’s heels, OpenAI introduced its personal assistants: Dots. They come with a family of brightly colored, globular mascot faces that float across your screen and converse with you. OpenAI says Dots will “bring you work done the way you would do it, sometimes before you even think to ask.”

Startups are making the same bet. The promotional material for Pickle, a personal AI app embodied in a floating, purple, three-dimensional animal that has big, inquisitive eyes, says that people will talk more, and share more, with “something alive you grow attached to that remembers your life and eventually acts alongside you.”

Although cute designs are not inherently sinister, they can make unfamiliar technology feel much more accessible and comforting. Cuteness can also obscure the invasive potential of AI agents, soften how users perceive risks such as extensive data collection and surveillance, and distract people into allowing agents to act on their behalf without clear consent.

We are scholars of digital technologies, and we have spent years researching the language and messaging companies use to represent technologies. We believe that this sleight of hand of marketing high-tech goods in a disarming package may be the greatest power of cuteness, and tech companies appear to be harnessing it to encourage people to adopt AI.

Presenting new technologies as cute is nothing new. Hello Kitty, Labubus, Tamagotchis and other products have famously promoted cuteness to evoke emotional attachment in consumers. They were just collectibles, however, and largely harmless. They couldn’t read an owner’s messages, access an owner’s accounts or act for them. When the cute thing is an AI agent, however, the stakes are much higher.

We have shown how particular ways of talking about technology can influence perceptions of safety and make dangers of technologies less visible. “Cutewashing” can mask privacy concerns and drive adoption by many people, creating a mass market.
Cute things can make you feel happy, trusting, affectionate or protective, encouraging you to form emotional connections with a technology.

Big Tech, in particular, has long embraced a virtual menagerie of cute animals. Silicon Valley has given the world the Firefox Fox, now-defunct Gateway cows, the former Twitter bird, GitHub’s octopus, Mailchimp’s monkey and Hootsuite’s owl. The perceived innocence of creatures can soften how people perceive the consequences of innovation.

AI companies are pursuing what some researchers have referred to as the “cute economy” to make money as well. Feelings generated through cuteness can build brand loyalty and encourage people to keep engaging with the products. Cuteness can function as a marketing strategy, too, as users become emotionally invested in a product. This, in turn, can influence purchases.

Research also shows that people confide in a friendly character more than a plain tool, sharing moods, routines, relationships and preferences. People will grant friendly agents access to their messages, calendars and accounts, yielding far richer data that the agent’s company can plumb than is usually obtained by a routine chatbot. Cuteness can lower skepticism so people are more likely to grant broad permissions and less likely to read the fine print. Attachment also makes it more difficult for users to leave an agent.

Making a technology cute can influence what people notice about it and what they overlook. A charming AI assistant may seem more approachable and less threatening, potentially drawing attention away from questions about data collection, privacy, security and surveillance. In one example, Muse has read a user’s text messages and given out another’s home address without the users’ knowledge.

To help people take a more cautious view of cute AI agents, we believe that companies should clearly explain to users what an agent can access, what it can do and who benefits. Disclosures and privacy policies should be stated in plain language, not dense legalese.

In the meantime, before you adopt an agent, ask what data it can access and what it can do with that access. It’s important to avoid letting cuteness be a distraction from the consequences of using the technology.
Jessica Maddox is affiliated with the American Influencer Council.

articles.title: It’s a bumper year for wild mushrooms – here’s what you could find in the woods today
articles.author: Joni Wildman, PhD Candidate in Mycology, University of Bath
paras: This autumn looks like it could be a good year to spot large numbers of wild mushrooms. Already many can be seen covering tree roots and shady spots.

Mushrooms are the part of certain fungi that you see above ground. The rest of it is either underground or within a tree trunk. All mushrooms are part of a fungus, but not all fungi produce mushrooms. There are believed to be 14,000 species of mushroom, and 140,000 of fungi.

To observe what was growing and what wasn’t this autumn, I recently joined a fungi walk in a Somerset woodland. Fungi were everywhere. Our group could barely cover half a kilometre in an hour because there was so much to stop and examine.

Among our sightings were large numbers of bright yellow stagshorn fungi (Calocera viscosa), coral-like clusters emerging from green moss, alongside vivid purple Russulas and more unusual specimens including one looking like a felty black tongue (seen in photo below), which we took for microscopic identification.

Our small group of fungi researchers recorded 39 different fungi. There’s nothing more magical than the iconic red-and-white fly agarics (Amanita muscaria), and our noted observations helped to set a nationwide record for the most of this type recorded in a single day at 276.

Another fungus showing off its colours this year is chicken of the woods (Laetioporus sulphureus). Look out for its cascading, bright yellow lobes bursting from urban trees. Sightings on the citizen science platform iNaturalist of this mushroom have increased by around 25% in the UK, compared with the same period last year.
The mushroom season could be about to get even better. Studies on mushroom production in pine forests have identified rainfall as among the strongest predictors of annual productivity.

Higher temperatures can limit production early in the season but help extend it later. A damp autumn, with enough warmth remaining, could therefore provide excellent mushroom weather. And that is precisely what the UK Met Office is forecasting. With a strengthening El Niño in the Pacific, the chances of a warm, wet autumn in the UK are estimated to be around 1.5 times higher than normal. For fungi emerging from a dry summer, this is good news.

Mushrooms are the temporary fruit that fungi produce for reproduction. The main part of the fungus remains hidden and is a network of tube-like filaments called mycelium, which can come together to form a developing mushroom.
The fungus then has a clever way of using water pressure within its cells to expand this structure and push it above ground, a little like inflating a balloon.
This helps explain why mushrooms often pop up after rain. They need plenty of moisture to grow, and the mushroom “balloon” you see can be up to 90% water.
But more mushrooms don’t always mean healthier ecosystems. An abundance of certain fungi can signal ecosystems under stress.

The long, dry summer has stressed vegetation, potentially leaving trees more vulnerable to pathogens such as honey fungus (Armillaria sp.). These fungi attack living tree roots, sometimes killing their hosts, and produce mushrooms in enormous honey-coloured clusters having done so.
In the dry summer of 2025, the Royal Horticultural Society reported a 43% rise in enquiries about garden fungi, most commonly honey fungus.

Meanwhile, fungi that recycle nutrients by breaking down dead organic matter may have an unusually abundant supply of drought-stricken vegetation to feast on. Another side effect of the very dry summer.

But some species are struggling. Many fungi rely on partnerships with living trees, exchanging nutrients and water for sugars produced through photosynthesis. For these species, vegetation productivity can strongly predict mushroom yield. Drought affecting their host trees may therefore have consequences that autumn rain cannot immediately reverse.

Others need suitable soil conditions to develop their underground mycelium, before producing mushrooms. Some soils in the UK remain exceptionally dry this autumn, requiring substantial rainfall to restore moisture.

Waxcaps, for example, are grassland fungi appearing in extraordinary colours, from pink and yellow to green, with some even smelling of garlic. Associated with long-established, nutrient-poor grasslands, they are valuable indicators of ecological quality.
Prolonged drought could affect their underground mycelium, potentially limiting fruiting even when rain returns. Returning to the balloon analogy, there may simply be nothing to inflate.

October 2026 has seen a 36.6% drop in overall fungi recordings in the UK, compared to October 2025, according to iNaturalist records. However, the season is not yet over, so it’s not yet clear how things will pan out.

To observe the latest growth, head to your local woodland or grassland, pick up a field guide or join a guided walk. You don’t need to identify everything to appreciate it, and while no UK mushrooms are dangerous to touch, never eat one unless you’re absolutely certain of its identity.

This autumn’s abundance may have prompted some commercial pickers to sweep through woods picking large numbers of fungi. The Woodland Trust, a charity, has warned this can put wildlife under pressure as they are a source of food for animals such as deer and support the soil’s health. While foraging for personal use is allowed, picking for commercial sale is illegal.
By recording your finds through citizen science projects such as iNaturalist, you can also help experts understand which species are flourishing and which are struggling in a changing climate.
If the forecast threatens your outdoor plans this autumn, remember what might soon be popping up after the rain. This might just be the year you discover some remarkable mushrooms for yourself.
